unitDescription.value: In this unit, students use Micro:bit devices to explore data, communication and physical computing in a practical and age-appropriate context. Students learn how Microbits collect, transmit and represent data, with a focus on radio communication, binary representation and basic data security concepts. Through guided investigations, students explore how data can be gathered from sensors, transmitted between devices and analysed to identify patterns and trends. In the second part of the unit, students apply these skills to design and create wearable technologies, combining computational thinking, data analysis and ethical considerations when collecting data about people.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: In Digital Technologies, students should have frequent opportunities for authentic learning by making key connections with other learning areas.

description.value: In this assessment, students complete a written exam that assesses their understanding of how Microbits communicate and represent data. Students explain the differences between broadcast and direct radio communication, and demonstrate their understanding of how text, numbers and messages are represented using integers and binary. The exam also assesses students’ ability to model and reason about structured data, design and trace basic algorithms, and predict program outputs related to Microbit communication and simple encryption. This assessment provides evidence of students’ conceptual understanding of data transmission, representation and algorithmic thinking.

description.value: In this assessment, students design and develop a wearable Microbit-based solution to collect and analyse data related to a given investigation task. Students plan how data will be gathered using appropriate sensors, design algorithms to collect and store the data, and use digital tools to analyse and visualise results to draw conclusions. They select suitable hardware, design the user experience, manage the project process and evaluate their solution against design criteria and user needs. Students also demonstrate responsible and ethical data collection practices, reflecting on the purpose and impact of their digital solution.

activities.title: Key Vocabulary: Data and Information
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the distinction between raw data and structured information. Model how a raw numeric output from a sensor (e.g. '28') lacks utility until contextualised with a unit, location, and timestamp (e.g. '28°C recorded at St Brendan's College oval at 10:15 am'). Introduce Assessment 2 (Week 7 Data Exam) to emphasize that defining and classifying data representations accurately is an examinable QCAA standard.
activities.studentsDo: Read the terms in column 1 of the workbook table. Review the definition bank below the table and write the matching definition letter in the blank Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the definition bank below your table. Write the correct letter in the Match column beside each term.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is the number '104' classified as data rather than information?
expected: It is an uncontextualised raw value without units or labels indicating whether it represents heart rate, speed, or temperature.
question: How does adding context transform a raw reading into information?
expected: Context provides units, time, and meaning, allowing users to make an informed decision or interpretation.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Data: Raw, unorganised, and unprocessed facts, figures, symbols, or numeric readings collected without context.
- Information: Data that has been processed, contextualised, and structured so that it is meaningful and actionable for human decision-making.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the distinction between raw data and information, let us examine how a local organisation collects civic data to make municipal decisions.

lessons.title: Micro:bit as a Data Collection Device
lessons.learningGoal: Explain the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model by identifying the hardware components and sensor pathways of a Micro:bit.

orientate.smartStart: Examine the Micro:bit v2 displayed on the board. Without touching your physical device, identify one component that receives data from the outside world and one component that displays or outputs data.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can identify the input, processing, and output capabilities of a Micro:bit device

activities.title: Micro:bit Anatomy and Hardware Identification
activities.teacherDoes: Distribute unplugged Micro:bit v2 boards to student pairs. Project a high-resolution technical schematic showing both front and rear faces. Explicitly teach the four core hardware functional roles: Input, Processor, Output, and Edge Connector. Model identifying Callout 1 (5x5 Red LED Matrix) as an output device, Callout 2 (Push Button A) as a digital input, Callout 3 (Edge Connector Pins) as an input/output interface, and Callout 4 (Nordic nRF52833 Microprocessor) as the central processing unit.
activities.studentsDo: Inspect your physical Micro:bit device. Locate the four numbered components indicated on the projected diagram and complete the callout annotation fields in your workbook, identifying the component name and its system role.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine your physical Micro:bit. Fill in the callout fields for numbers 1 to 4 with the component name and its system role (Input, Process, or Output).
activities.questioning:
Which physical component on the Micro:bit interprets program logic and processes raw sensor values? Expected: The central microprocessor located on the rear of the board.
Why is Button A classified strictly as an input device? Expected: It detects an external physical event (mechanical push) and sends an electrical signal into the processor.
activities.scaffolding:
Hardware Functional Roles:
- Input: Collects signals or physical measurements from the environment (e.g. buttons, light sensor, accelerometer, temperature thermistor).
- Processor: Executes program instructions, performs logic operations, and manipulates stored values.
- Output: Displays results, produces sound, or transmits data to external devices (e.g. 5x5 LED matrix, onboard speaker, serial USB).
- Callout 1: 5x5 LED Matrix (Output)
- Callout 2: Push Button A (Input)
- Callout 3: Edge Connector Pins (Input/Output)
- Callout 4: Nordic Microprocessor (Process)
activities.eLearning: Rear-of-room monitoring while students inspect devices. Ensure devices remain unpowered on desks.
activities.transition: Now that we have labelled the physical hardware components, let us classify each onboard sensor and component systematically into the Input-Process-Output model.

workbookSpec.prompt: Identify each numbered hardware component and write its name and system role (Input, Process, or Output).
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Callout 1: 5x5 LED Matrix (Output). Callout 2: Push Button A (Input). Callout 3: Edge Connector Pins (Input/Output). Callout 4: Central Microprocessor (Process).

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Callout 1: 5x5 LED Matrix - Visual output display for characters, numbers, and pixel icons.
Callout 2: Push Button A - Digital push-button input sensor detecting user interaction.
Callout 3: Edge Connector Pins - Input/Output interface pins connecting external sensors and circuits.
Callout 4: Central Microprocessor (CPU) - Executes stored instructions and processes incoming sensor data.

activities.title: Hardware Classification: Input, Process, Output
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that every digital computing device operates on the Input-Process-Output (IPO) architecture. Walk students through five common Micro:bit components: Buttons A & B, 5x5 LED Screen, Central Microprocessor, Onboard Temperature Sensor (die thermistor), and Accelerometer/Motion Sensor. Model how to evaluate whether a component gathers data, processes logic, or presents a result. Guide students through classifying each component accurately into the workbook table.
activities.studentsDo: Review the five locked components in column 1 of your workbook table. In column 2, determine and record whether each component functions as an Input, Output, or Processor.
activities.visibleInstructions: Classify each locked Micro:bit component in your workbook table as either 'Input', 'Output', or 'Processor'.
activities.questioning:
question: Under which category does the internal temperature sensor fall, and what physical property does it detect?
expected: Input; it measures ambient heat from the physical environment and feeds electrical signals to the CPU.
question: If an accelerometer detects a sudden change in motion or a shake, is it acting as an input or an output?
expected: Input, because it receives mechanical force from the environment and passes that data into the program.
activities.scaffolding:
IPO Reference Definitions:
- Input: Gathers environmental or user stimuli.
- Processor: Evaluates conditions, executes calculations, and triggers actions.
- Output: Translates digital state into physical light, sound, or data signals.
activities.transition: Now that we have classified each component, let us map the sequential flow of data as it travels through a complete Micro:bit automated system.

activities.title: Mapping the Sensor Data Flow
activities.teacherDoes: Model tracing data through an automated temperature warning system. Walk through each stage on the whiteboard: Stage 1 represents the physical room environment; Stage 2 represents the sensor capturing analog heat and converting it into a numeric digital value; Stage 3 represents the microprocessor evaluating an 'if-else' conditional rule; and Stage 4 branches into two possible output actions based on whether the reading exceeds a 25°C threshold.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the sensor data journey flow diagram in your workbook by writing the missing operational descriptions for Stage 2 (Sensor Input) and Stage 3 (Processor Evaluation).
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the blank boxes in your workbook flow diagram to complete Stage 2 (Input) and Stage 3 (Processing logic).
activities.questioning:
What calculation or comparison must the microprocessor perform at Stage 3 before updating the display? Expected: It evaluates whether the temperature reading is greater than the set threshold value of 25°C.
What would happen to the output if the temperature sensor stopped collecting data? Expected: The processor would have no live input to evaluate, causing the display to freeze, show an error, or fail to branch correctly.
activities.scaffolding:
Flowchart Progression:
- Stage 1: Ambient room heat (Physical Environment).
- Stage 2: Temperature thermistor captures thermal reading as an integer (Input).
- Stage 3: Microprocessor compares integer against condition: Is reading > 25? (Process).
- Stage 4 Branch: Yes path triggers Sun icon on LED screen; No path triggers Snowflake icon on LED screen.
activities.transition: Let us collect our workbooks and summarise our understanding of the IPO model before we move to live programming in Lesson 3.

lessons.title: First Code & Live Data Streaming to Excel
lessons.learningGoal: Construct an algorithmic program to collect and stream live sensor telemetry from a Micro:bit to Microsoft Excel via serial connection.

orientate.smartStart: Log into your laptop, connect your BBC Micro:bit to your USB port using the provided cable, and navigate to makecode.microbit.org. Ensure your device appears as a connected drive on your computer.

activities.title: I Do: Modelling Serial Data Transmission Syntax
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the construction of a serial telemetry program on MakeCode via the projector. Explain the difference between 'show number' (which merely renders text across the LED matrix) and 'serial write value' (which packages structured key-value pairs through the COM port to external spreadsheet software). Switch MakeCode to JavaScript view to highlight syntax: 'serial.writeValue("temp", input.temperature());' and 'basic.pause(500);'. Explicitly explain why a 500 millisecond delay is mandatory to throttle the serial buffer and prevent Excel telemetry crashes.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration on the projector. Examine the monospaced JavaScript snippet in your workbook and fill in the missing function and delay parameter in the code holes.
activities.visibleInstructions: Look at the projected JavaScript code. Fill in code holes {{1}} and {{2}} in your workbook snippet to complete the serial streaming script.
activities.questioning:
Why is 'serial write value' required instead of 'show number' when streaming data into a spreadsheet? Expected: Serial write transmits structured key-value data packets over the USB connection that external software can parse into columns, whereas show number only displays digits on the LED screen.
What is the operational risk of running a serial write block in a forever loop without a pause delay? Expected: The Micro:bit floods the serial buffer with thousands of messages per second, causing the receiving application to freeze or drop data.
activities.eLearning: Project MakeCode editor. Ensure students' laptop screens are angled at 45 degrees while code syntax is modelled.
activities.transition: Now that we have modelled the script structure and completed our syntax notes, let us pair our physical Micro:bits and configure the Excel Data Streamer add-in.

activities.title: We Do: Guided Connection and Telemetry Streaming
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students step-by-step through compiling their MakeCode program and transferring the compiled .hex file onto the connected Micro:bit drive. Model opening Microsoft Excel, enabling the 'Data Streamer' tab via Excel Options (File > Options > Add-ins > COM Add-ins > Microsoft Data Streamer for Excel), selecting 'Connect a Device', choosing the active USB Serial COM port, and clicking 'Start Data'. Confirm that rows of live data begin streaming continuously into the Data In worksheet.

activities.visibleInstructions: Complete each setup milestone with the teacher. Tick off each procedural checkbox in your workbook once confirmed on your screen.
activities.questioning:
q: If Excel displays 'Device disconnected' or does not populate readings, what is our primary diagnostic check?
Expected: Verify the USB cable is firmly connected, confirm the COM port in Data Streamer matches the Micro:bit, and ensure the code was properly flashed.
q: How does Excel organise the incoming serial packet?
Expected: It splits the transmitted key-value pair into labelled header columns with automatic timestamps.

Connection Milestones:

2. In Excel, verify 'Data Streamer' appears in the top ribbon (Add-ins menu).
3. Click 'Connect a Device' and choose 'BBC micro:bit'.
4. Click 'Start Data' and verify incoming rows populate column values.

activities.title: You Do: Physical Sensor Testing and Data Logging
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate around the room to troubleshoot COM port drops and assist students in observing telemetry shifts in Excel. Demonstrate testing technique: 'Hold your thumb firmly against the central microprocessor on the back of the Micro:bit. Watch cell C5 in your Excel sheet rise from ~23°C to ~31°C.' Direct students to record their baseline and stimulated temperature readings into their workbook tables.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct physical tests on your Micro:bit sensor: record the baseline classroom temperature in Excel, warm the processor chip with your thumb, and gently blow air across the board. Log the observed numeric temperatures (°C) from Excel into the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the live values streaming in your Excel worksheet. Record the observed temperature (°C) for each of the three physical test conditions in your workbook table.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does the temperature reading take several seconds to decline after removing your thumb?
expected: The processor casing retains residual thermal energy that gradually dissipates back to room temperature.
question: How does viewing data in tabular Excel rows improve our ability to detect trends compared to reading numbers off the Micro:bit LED screen?
expected: Excel records chronological history with timestamps in rows, allowing us to see minimum, maximum, and rate of change over time.
activities.scaffolding:
Physical Testing Protocol:
- Condition 1 (Ambient): Rest device flat on desk untouched for 30 seconds; record stable reading.
- Condition 2 (Warmed): Hold thumb firmly over the rear CPU chip for 20 seconds; record peak reading.
- Condition 3 (Cooled): Remove thumb and gently blow air across the chip surface; record stabilized reading.
Expected ranges: Ambient ~21–24°C; Warmed ~28–34°C; Cooled ~20–23°C.
activities.eLearning: Students work independently in Excel while teacher conducts rear-of-room monitoring for device connectivity and data logging.

activities.title: Vocabulary of Data Types
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the three foundational data types for wearable computing: Numerical, Categorical, and Boolean. Model an example from the Yeppoon Seagulls Rugby League GPS telemetry: heart rate (numerical), player position (categorical), and in-play state (Boolean). Emphasise that spreadsheet algorithms rely on correct data typing to perform mathematical operations.
activities.studentsDo: Match each data type in the workbook table to its correct definition from the bank by writing the matching definition letter.
activities.visibleInstructions: Look at the key terms in your workbook. Use the definition bank to write the matching definition for Numerical, Categorical, and Boolean data.
activities.questioning:
Why is a player jersey number classified as categorical rather than numerical? Expected: It serves as an identifier label; adding or averaging jersey numbers does not produce a meaningful mathematical result.
What data type is generated if a wearable heart sensor outputs True when maximum heart rate is exceeded and False otherwise? Expected: Boolean, because it only has two possible binary states.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions in bank:
- Numerical: Measurable values expressed as numbers that can be mathematically operated on or averaged.
- Categorical: Labelled categories or groups that sort items into qualitative classes.
- Boolean: Logical binary data containing only one of two possible states (True/False, 1/0).
activities.eLearning: Project the vocabulary slide at the front while monitoring workbook responses from the rear of the classroom.
activities.transition: Now that we have formal definitions for each data type, let's examine raw telemetry feeds from smartwatch sensors.

activities.title: Anatomy of Structured Tables
activities.teacherDoes: Project a clean weather telemetry log from Keppel Bay Marina. Explicitly define and illustrate the core structural elements of a flat database: Record (Row), Attribute (Column), Header, and Data Integrity. Model why entering measurement units such as '24°C' into a cell breaks calculation rules: 'Spreadsheets read letters as strings, stripping away numeric mathematical properties.'
activities.studentsDo: Examine the definitions provided in the bank and match each structural spreadsheet term in column 1 to its correct definition in the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each spreadsheet structure term (Record, Attribute, Header, Data Integrity) to its definition from the bank in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the structural difference between a row and a column in a relational spreadsheet?
expected: A row represents an individual observation or record, whereas a column represents a specific attribute measured across all records.
question: Why must measurement units like °C or metres be kept strictly in the header?
expected: Putting units inside cells converts numbers into text strings, preventing formulas like SUM or AVERAGE from calculating.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions in bank:
- Record: A single horizontal row containing all attribute readings for one specific observation event.
- Attribute: A vertical column holding values for a single characteristic across all records.
- Header: The top label row that identifies each attribute and declares its unit of measurement.
- Data Integrity: The accuracy, consistency, and validity of data stored across the entire dataset.
activities.transition: Now that we know the anatomy of a valid table, let's audit a poorly formatted environmental log from Livingstone Shire Council.

activities.title: Auditing Dataset Violations
activities.teacherDoes: Display a flawed marina water-quality dataset on the projector containing three glaring violations: units typed into cell values (e.g. '18.4 knots'), blank rows interspersed between entries, and inconsistent date-time stamps. Model auditing error 1: 'Notice cell B3 contains knots inside the cell. I record this as a unit violation that destroys numeric formatting.' Deliver the core concept clearly, ensuring students understand that spreadsheets rely on strict schema rules to maintain data integrity.
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the projected flawed dataset and record the three specific data integrity errors in the workbook, explaining how each error impairs spreadsheet operations using structured written sections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Identify three distinct structural errors in the displayed marina dataset. In your workbook, record each error and explain how it damages data integrity using the provided sections.
activities.questioning:
How do blank rows inside a dataset affect automated functions in Excel?
Expected: Blank rows break the contiguous range, causing sorting, filtering, and autofill formulas to stop prematurely.
Why does inconsistent timestamp formatting (e.g. mixing 12-hour and 24-hour time) disrupt data analysis?
Expected: Spreadsheets cannot correctly order or plot time-series records sequentially when formats conflict.
activities.scaffolding:
Common integrity violations checklist:
1. Units appended to numeric cell values (prevents arithmetic).
2. Empty rows or columns splitting data tables (breaks auto-selection).
3. Inconsistent format syntax (e.g. DD/MM vs text dates).

workbookSpec.title: Dataset Integrity Audit

activities.title: Pillars of Data Quality Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the three primary pillars of data quality: Accuracy, Consistency, and Completeness. Demonstrate on the main display using a mock Micro:bit temperature log: 950°C violates accuracy; alternating between 'deg C' and 'Celsius' violates consistency; a missing reading in a 5-second interval violates completeness. Instruct students to match the terms to their definitions in their workbooks.
activities.studentsDo: Read each term in the left column and write the matching definition from the bank into the blank Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each of the 3 data quality terms to its correct definition from the bank below.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is an impossible sensor value of 950°C classified as an accuracy issue rather than a consistency issue?
Expected: Because it represents a value that is physically untrue to real-world conditions, rather than a formatting mismatch.
question: How could a dataset be completely consistent yet entirely inaccurate?
Expected: All entries could be formatted identically as numbers with units, but the sensor calibration could be incorrect, making all values wrong.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
Accuracy: The degree to which recorded data matches real-world truth.
Consistency: Uniform representation, measurement units, and formatting across the entire dataset.
Completeness: The presence of all expected data entries without missing records or null fields.

activities.title: Causes of Sensor Data Errors
activities.teacherDoes: Present the four main root causes of bad data in wearable computing: Calibration Drift (hardware drift over time), Transmission Noise (serial signal dropouts or baud rate spikes), Outliers (sporadic electrical interference), and Human Error (manual logging errors). Model filling in the missing technical terms on the guided notes cloze activity by demonstrating how context clues within the sentence structure determine the correct vocabulary choice.

activities.questioning:
question: What causes transmission noise when streaming data from a Micro:bit via USB serial?
expected: A loose physical connection or a serial buffer overflow when data is written faster than the logging software can process.
question: Why must extreme outliers be investigated before simply deleting them from a sensor dataset?
expected: An outlier might represent a genuine physical event—such as a high-impact tackle in a St Brendan's rugby match—rather than a sensor malfunction.
activities.scaffolding:
Word bank terms:
- calibration: mechanical baseline alignment of hardware.
- transmission: digital relay of data packets over cables or radio.
- outliers: values sitting drastically outside normal ranges.
- human: manual typing or incorrect unit entry.
- integrity: overall trustworthiness and reliability of data.

activities.title: Validation Rule Types & Definitions
activities.teacherDoes: Define data validation as automated boundary checks implemented at the point of data entry at St Brendan's College. Contrast reactive data cleaning (fixing corrupt data after the fact) with proactive data validation (preventing corrupt data entry). Define the three primary validation types: Range Limits, List Constraints, and Data Type Constraints. Model real-world wearable tech examples for Yeppoon Seagulls Rugby League athletes.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the workbook table by matching each validation constraint type with its definition from the bank, and review the Yeppoon Seagulls athlete tracking use cases.

activities.questioning:
Why is a list constraint more effective than an open text box for recording an SBC House or sports team?
Expected: It eliminates typos, trailing spaces, and case differences by only allowing pre-approved selections.
What error occurs if an athlete's step count is validated as a whole number but someone enters '4,500.5'?
Expected: A type constraint violation, because a decimal value is not an integer.
activities.scaffolding:
Constraint definitions:
- Range limit: Restricts numerical values to a defined minimum and maximum threshold.
- List constraint: Restricts text values to an explicit list of allowed items.
- Type constraint: Restricts entries to specific structural formats (e.g., Integer, Decimal, Date, Text).

Write the definitions on the board and model how to identify each concept using a sample line of logged Micro:bit temperature data collected from a student running on the St Brendan's College oval. prompt: How does an overall trend differ from a repeating pattern?
Expected: A trend shows a continuous directional shift (upward or downward) over a given timeframe, whereas a pattern is a recurring cyclical sequence.

culminate.smartFinish: On your workbook exit slip, write down: 1 key trend identified in today's dataset, and 1 diagnostic reason why anomalies must be flagged before drawing conclusions.
culminate.summarise: We defined trends, patterns, and anomalies, and demonstrated how time-series sensor data reveals physical changes over time when anomalies are separated.
culminate.nextSteps: Next lesson we will learn how to choose the correct visual representation—line graphs versus column graphs—for different types of Micro:bit datasets.

lessons.title: Introduction to Binary Representation
lessons.learningGoal: Convert decimal numbers into 4-bit and 8-bit binary integers to explain how digital systems store numerical data.

orientate.smartStart: On the board, display the decimal value 13 alongside four electrical switch icons (Off, On, On, Off). Ask students to write down on their mini-whiteboards or scrap paper how many electrical states a digital switch possesses and why a computer cannot directly store the digit '9'.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can convert decimal integers into binary numbers and explain how computers store data using two electrical states

activities.title: Binary Computing Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly explain that digital microprocessors like the Micro:bit do not understand human base-10 digits; they operate exclusively via transistor voltage thresholds (high voltage = 1, low voltage = 0). Define bit, byte, binary (base-2), and decimal (base-10). Model on the whiteboard: 1 bit = a single 0 or 1; 1 byte = a cluster of 8 bits. Emphasise that all wearable telemetry (heart rate, step counts, temperature) must be encoded into these binary patterns.
activities.studentsDo: In the workbook vocabulary matching table, review the four locked computing terms and write the matching definition letter from the definition bank into the blank Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Look at the four terms in your workbook table. Read the definition bank below the table and write the matching definition letter next to each term in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do digital microcontrollers like the Micro:bit rely exclusively on binary instead of decimal digits 0 to 9?
Expected: Transistors and electronic circuits operate most reliably in two discrete physical states (high voltage / on vs low voltage / off), which eliminates electrical ambiguity.
q: What is the fundamental difference between a bit and a byte?
Expected: A bit is a single binary digit (0 or 1), whereas a byte is a group of 8 bits used as a standard unit of storage.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
• Bit: The smallest atomic unit of digital data, holding either a 0 or a 1.
• Byte: A standard addressable unit of digital data comprised of 8 bits.
• Binary: A base-2 positional number system utilizing only two digits: 0 and 1.
• Decimal: A base-10 positional number system utilizing ten digits: 0 through 9.
activities.eLearning: Project the vocabulary table on the front board. Ensure all student laptops remain closed while definitions are introduced.
activities.transition: Instruct students to check their letter matches with their desk partner before we unpack the positional place values of binary.

workbookSpec.title: Digital Representation Vocabulary
workbookSpec.prompt: Match each computing term in the left column to its correct definition from the bank below.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Bit (b) matches A; Byte (B) matches B; Binary matches C; Decimal matches D.
bank: A: The smallest atomic unit of digital data, representing a single binary digit (0 or 1).
B: A standardized grouping of 8 bits used to represent characters and numerical values.
C: A base-2 numbering system where values are expressed using combinations of 0 and 1.
D: A base-10 numbering system used in everyday human mathematics consisting of digits 0–9.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Bit (b) = A; Byte (B) = B; Binary = C; Decimal = D

activities.title: Positional Notation & Place Value Rules
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the mathematical structure of positional notation on the board. Contrast decimal powers of 10 (100, 10, 1) with binary powers of 2 (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1). Model how each bit's position doubles in magnitude moving right to left. Walk through the cloze passage sentence-by-sentence, calling on students to identify which term from the word bank logically completes the rule. Modelled example: 'Unlike the decimal system which is base-10, binary is a base-2 system...' Emphasise how this maps directly to transistor voltage states in the Micro:bit processor.
activities.studentsDo: Follow along with the direct instruction and complete the cloze sentences in the workbook using the provided word bank. Verify that the place-value sequence 8-4-2-1 is correctly identified in their notes before moving to calculations.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill each numbered blank in the guided notes using the terms from the word bank. Ensure each word is used exactly once to complete the explanation of binary place value.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does the value of each successive binary column double as you move from right to left?
expected: Because binary is a base-2 system, each place value represents an increasing power of 2 (2^0=1, 2^1=2, 2^2=4, 2^3=8).
question: What would the next column to the left of the 8s place represent in a 5-bit number?
expected: The 16s place (2^4 = 16).
activities.scaffolding:
Binary Place Value Progression:
2^3 = 8
2^2 = 4
2^1 = 2
2^0 = 1
Summation Rule: Decimal Value = (Bit × 8) + (Bit × 4) + (Bit × 2) + (Bit × 1). Transistor States: Off = 0V to 0.8V, On = 2V to 3.3V.
activities.eLearning: Display the interactive place-value chart on the main projector.
activities.transition: Direct students to turn to the conversion grid in their workbook to apply these place values to actual decimal numbers.

workbookSpec.text: Unlike the decimal system which is base-10, binary is a {{1}} system that relies on only two digits: 0 and 1. In a digital circuit, a 0 indicates an {{2}} state, while a 1 indicates an {{3}} state. Each digit's magnitude is determined by its {{4}}, which doubles as you move from right to left. To calculate the total value of a 4-bit binary sequence, you must calculate the {{5}} of all active columns.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. base-2
2. off
3. on
4. place value
5. sum

activities.title: Generative Binary Conversion Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Model the subtraction / greedy algorithm for decimal-to-binary conversion using the decimal number 11: Does 8 fit into 11? Yes (put 1, remainder 3). Does 4 fit into 3? No (put 0, remainder 3). Does 2 fit into 3? Yes (put 1, remainder 1). Does 1 fit into 1? Yes (put 1, remainder 0). Final 4-bit binary: 1011. Circulate around the classroom, verifying students place 1s and 0s accurately in the columns.
activities.studentsDo: Calculate and complete the binary conversion matrix in the workbook for decimal values 3, 6, 9, 13, and 15, recording 1 or 0 in each place value column (8, 4, 2, 1) and writing the final 4-bit binary code.
activities.visibleInstructions: Calculate the binary code for each decimal integer in the table. Place a 1 in the column if that power of two is used, or a 0 if it is not. Write the complete 4-bit binary code in the rightmost column.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the absolute maximum decimal value that can be represented using a 4-bit binary number?
expected: 15, because 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 (1111 in binary).
question: What happens if a sensor attempts to store the decimal integer 16 in a 4-bit register?
expected: An overflow error occurs because 16 requires a fifth bit (the 16s column, 10000).
activities.scaffolding:
Worked Example: Decimal 7
• 8s place: 0 (7 < 8)
• 4s place: 1 (7 - 4 = 3)
• 2s place: 1 (3 - 2 = 1)
• 1s place: 1 (1 - 1 = 0)
Binary Code: 0111

lessons.title: Binary and Micro:bit Sensor Telemetry
lessons.learningGoal: Calculate 8-bit binary sensor representations and evaluate Boolean threshold states for Micro:bit wearable technology.

orientate.smartStart: Display a quick retrieval problem on the screen: 'What is the binary value of the decimal number 10?' Give students 60 seconds to solve it using an 8-4-2-1 table, then cold-call two students for the answer (1010).
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how Micro:bit sensors convert analogue signals into 8-bit digital integers and Boolean flags

activities.title: Analogue-to-Digital Conversion & 8-Bit Scaling
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that physical sensors (e.g. Micro:bit light level sensor or temperature sensor) detect continuous analogue physical signals. Demonstrate how the internal Analogue-to-Digital Converter (ADC) samples this continuous electrical voltage and quantises it into an 8-bit integer ranging from 0 (total darkness / 0V) to 255 (maximum brightness / 3.3V). Model the bit depth formula: 2^8 = 256 unique steps. Show how the light reading 65 is represented as 8-bit binary: 01000001 (64 + 1).
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's mathematical modeling in their workbooks and complete the structured written response detailing sensor resolution, the 8-bit formula, and the conversion calculation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the three sections in your workbook: write the definition of an ADC, calculate the range of an 8-bit integer, and convert the sensor reading 65 into an 8-bit binary byte.
activities.questioning: Why can an 8-bit sensor register values only between 0 and 255 rather than 1 to 256? Expected: In digital computing, indexing begins at 0, meaning 0 represents the first value and 255 represents the 256th discrete state. What would happen to the precision of a wearable heart-rate sensor if we upgraded from an 8-bit ADC to a 10-bit ADC? Expected: Sensor precision would increase significantly because 2^10 allows 1024 distinct measurement levels instead of only 256.
activities.scaffolding:
Reference Notes:
• ADC (Analogue-to-Digital Converter): Converts continuous physical voltage into discrete digital numbers.
• 8-bit range formula: 2^8 = 256 possible values (0 through 255).
• 8-bit Place Values: 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
• Example conversion for 65: 0×128 + 1×64 + 0×32 + 0×16 + 0×8 + 0×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 01000001.
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate the MakeCode Micro:bit simulator on the projector showing live light level changes between 0 and 255.
activities.transition: Instruct students to shift their focus from raw 8-bit integers to binary logic flags and conditional statements.

workbookSpec.title: Micro:bit Sensor Quantisation & Bit Depth
workbookSpec.prompt: Document how physical sensor readings are converted into digital values and calculate 8-bit sensor representation.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. ADC Function: Samples continuous physical analogue voltages from the sensor and converts them into discrete numerical integers for the microcontroller.
2. Bit-Depth: 2^8 = 256 discrete values. Because counting begins at 0 in computing, the range spans from 0 to 255.
3. Worked Calculation: 65 = 64 + 1. In 8 bits (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1), this is 01000001.

activities.title: Sensor Thresholds & Boolean Logic Mapping
activities.teacherDoes: Model how wearable devices conserve processor cycles and memory by reducing complex sensor telemetry into single-bit Boolean flags (1 = True / Triggered; 0 = False / Inactive). Co-construct the first two rows of the sensor logic table on the board: evaluate a temperature sensor reading of 28°C against a safety threshold of > 25°C (Condition met = True / 1). Guide students through evaluating light and button states.
activities.studentsDo: Work collaboratively with the teacher to analyse the four wearable sensor scenarios, ticking whether the condition is met and writing the corresponding binary value (1 or 0) in the table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine each sensor condition in the table. Tick the box if the threshold condition evaluates to True, and record the binary digit (1 or 0) in the right-hand column.
activities.questioning:
question: If a wearable fitness band checks if a user's step count has reached the 10,000-step daily target, why does it store this status as a single bit rather than text?
Expected: Storing a single bit (1 for True, 0 for False) uses minimal memory and can be evaluated instantly by processor logic gates.
question: What electrical state inside the Micro:bit does binary 1 represent?
Expected: High voltage (typically 3.3V in Micro:bit circuitry).
activities.scaffolding:
Threshold Evaluation Rules:
• True Condition = Threshold reached -> Binary 1 (High / Active)
• False Condition = Threshold not reached -> Binary 0 (Low / Inactive)
Scenario 1: Light = 42; Threshold < 50. 42 < 50 is TRUE -> Tick -> Binary 1.
Scenario 2: Temp = 36.8°C; Threshold > 38.0°C. 36.8 > 38.0 is FALSE -> No tick -> Binary 0.

sections.label: Question 1 (Calculate): Show full place-value working to convert decimal 14 into 4-bit binary, and binary 1010 into decimal.

activities.workbookMaterials: Written: Data Representation Exam Practice Items
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Question 1:
• Decimal 14 to 4-bit binary: 14 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 0. Place values (8, 4, 2, 1) -> 1110.
• Binary 1010 to decimal: (1×8) + (0×4) + (1×2) + (0×1) = 8 + 2 = 10.
Question 2:
• Microcontrollers utilize binary integers because hardware transistors operate via two electrical voltage states (high/1 and low/0). Storing readings as binary integers (e.g. an 8-bit byte for 0–255) consumes only 1 byte of memory and radio bandwidth, whereas storing '255' as decimal text requires 3 bytes (one ASCII byte per character). Binary representation therefore minimizes memory overhead, speeds up processing, and optimizes battery life in wearable devices.

activities.title: Defining Wireless Transmission Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Present the four core networking definitions on the board. Model the difference between 'Broadcast' and 'Direct' communication using classroom communication analogies: broadcast is an announcement across the PA system heard by every classroom; direct communication is like a targeted letter delivered solely to room 14. q: Why will two Micro:bits on different radio group IDs fail to communicate even if they are held 5 centimetres apart?
Expected: The Micro:bit firmware filters out and ignores any radio packets that do not match its assigned group ID.

Expected: Broadcast traffic collision and interference; messages will cross over and trigger handlers on everyone's screens.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Broadcast: Sending a packet across a frequency so every receiver in operational range can capture it.
- Direct Communication: Sending data addressed specifically to an individual device ID.
- Radio Group: A software channel (0–255) used to segment and filter wireless traffic.
- Packet Interference: Data collisions causing corrupted or unreadable transmissions when simultaneous signals share one channel.

workbookSpec.title: Radio Transmission & Filtering Principles
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the technical summary using terms from the word bank.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Micro:bit devices utilise radio waves to exchange information wirelessly. This process can occur in two main forms: broadcast communication and direct communication. When a Micro:bit operates in broadcast mode, it transmits a signal that can be received by any other Micro:bits within its transmission range, provided they share the same radio group. This method is comparable to a public radio station sending signals to all listeners. In contrast, direct communication involves sending data to a specific Micro:bit, often identified by a specific address or group setting. This approach enhances the privacy of data delivery and minimises potential interference from unrelated signals.

workbookSpec.title: Channel Filtering & Packet Delivery Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Document your observations when sender and receiver group IDs were mismatched, and explain the technical reason for the system behaviour.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: When the receiver group ID was changed, the sending device continued to broadcast packets, but the receiving Micro:bit displayed nothing on its LED matrix. This occurs because the radio group ID functions as a hardware/software filter. When radio waves hit the receiver's antenna, the device inspects the group ID in the packet header. Because the header ID does not match the receiver's configured group ID, the packet is instantly discarded before triggering the 'on radio received' event handler. Furthermore, because standard radio broadcast lacks an acknowledgement handshake, the sender has no awareness that its message failed to be processed.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Key points required in student response:
1. Accurate observation: No text displayed on receiver screen despite sender transmitting.
2. Technical mechanism: Receiver antenna captures physical wave, reads packet header, detects group mismatch, and drops/ignores packet.
3. Lack of acknowledgement: Sender has no mechanism to know delivery failed.

orientate.smartStart: Recall from Lesson 2: When your sender Micro:bit transmitted 'DATA_OK', how did it confirm that the receiver actually received the message? (Expected: It didn't; broadcast is one-way with no confirmation or receipt acknowledgement).
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how to make wireless data transmission reliable and secure

activities.title: Categorising Transmission Vulnerabilities
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define and contrast 'Reliability' and 'Security' in data communications. Reliability asks: 'Did the complete, accurate data actually arrive at the destination without loss or distortion?' Security asks: 'Was the data protected from unauthorised interception, reading, or tampering?' Present 4 real-world wearable tech scenarios and model how to audit each as either a reliability issue or a security threat. For instance, model Scenario 1: 'Physical distance causes radio packets to drop, resulting in missing telemetry entries. Because this stems from environmental attenuation rather than malicious intent or confidentiality breach, it is classified under Reliability.'
activities.studentsDo: Classify four distinct data communication challenges in the workbook table by ticking whether each represents a Reliability failure or a Security vulnerability.
activities.visibleInstructions: Read each transmission scenario in column 1. Determine whether the primary flaw impacts system Reliability or system Security, and place a tick in the corresponding column.
activities.questioning:
prompt: If a wearable fitness tracker drops 10 seconds of heart rate data while the runner passes under high-voltage power lines, is that a reliability or security flaw?
expected: Reliability flaw, because external electromagnetic interference caused packet loss, not unauthorised access.
prompt: If a spectator uses an open Micro:bit receiver to read and display a competitor's live heart rate telemetry, what principle is breached?
expected: Security (specifically data confidentiality and privacy).
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Reliability: Guaranteeing accurate, complete, and uncorrupted delivery of packets from sender to receiver.
- Security: Protecting data against unauthorised eavesdropping (sniffing), modification, or theft.
- Packet Loss: Physical drop-out of radio frames due to distance, obstacles, or collisions.
- Eavesdropping: Capturing unencrypted broadcast radio packets using an open receiver.
activities.transition: Review the classification audit as a class, then examine specific engineering strategies to mitigate both problems.

workbookSpec.title: Data Transmission Vulnerability Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Analyse each transmission scenario and tick whether it represents a failure of Reliability or Security.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Scenario 1: Reliability; Scenario 2: Security; Scenario 3: Reliability; Scenario 4: Security

rows.value: Physical distance causes radio packets to drop, resulting in missing telemetry entries.
An unauthorised receiver on the same channel intercepts and logs private athlete heart rate data.
Radio frequency interference flips bits during transit, producing corrupted sensor readings.
A malicious actor transmits spoofed sensor packets to alter scoreboard values on the receiver.

activities.workbookMaterials: Table auditing reliability versus security transmission scenarios.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Row 1 (Dropped packets from distance): Reliability tick checked.
Row 2 (Unauthorised interception of telemetry): Security tick checked.
Row 3 (Corrupted bits from interference): Reliability tick checked.
Row 4 (Malicious packet spoofing): Security tick checked.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Mitigation Protocols & Simple Encryption
activities.teacherDoes: Unpack the technical mechanisms used to address wireless transmission flaws: 1. Acknowledgement protocols (ACK/NACK handshakes) where the receiver confirms receipt, enabling the sender to retransmit if lost (improves reliability); 2. Redundancy and checksums (sending verification math alongside data); 3. Simple Encryption (scrambling the payload using a symmetric key/offset, such as a Caesar cipher, so eavesdroppers capture meaningless ciphertext). Model how these trade-offs affect low-power wearable devices on the board by drawing a timing diagram for an ACK handshake and calculating battery drain costs.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the structured guided notes table in the workbook, defining the operational purpose and trade-offs of ACK protocols, checksums, and simple encryption.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 3 mitigation strategy definitions in your workbook table, identifying how each strategy improves wireless communication.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the computational cost of implementing an acknowledgement protocol on a battery-powered wearable device?
expected: It doubles radio transmissions, keeping the radio transmitter active longer and draining battery faster.
question: If an eavesdropper intercepts an encrypted string like 'KHOOR' instead of 'HELLO', why does that solve the confidentiality problem even though the packet was captured?
expected: The attacker has captured the raw transmission, but without the secret key (shift -3), the data payload cannot be interpreted.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for notes:
- Acknowledgement (ACK): A return message sent by the receiver confirming packet arrival; triggers retransmission if missing.
- Parity / Checksum: A calculated verification number sent with data to detect if bits were corrupted during flight.
- Caesar / Substitution Cipher: A basic encryption method shifting alphabet characters by a fixed numeric key to conceal plain text.
activities.transition: Move directly to synthesising these insights into our checkpoint reflection ahead of the Week 7 Data Exam.

workbookSpec.title: Transmission Mitigation Strategies
workbookSpec.prompt: Define each technical mitigation strategy and state whether its primary purpose is ensuring reliability or security.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Row 1: Acknowledgement (ACK) Protocol - Reliability; Row 2: Error-Checking Checksum - Reliability; Row 3: Symmetric Substitution Cipher - Security

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Row 1 (Acknowledgement): Mechanism where receiver transmits an 'ACK' packet back upon receipt. If timeout expires without ACK, sender retransmits. Ensures transmission Reliability.
Row 2 (Checksum): Mathematical value appended to data allowing receiver to recalculate and verify bits did not corrupt in transit. Ensures transmission Reliability.
Row 3 (Payload Encryption): Encoding plaintext data using a secret algorithm/key before transmission so intercepted packets cannot be read by unauthorised third parties. Ensures transmission Security.

activities.questioning: Why is an open radio broadcast channel fundamentally insecure for transmitting medical telemetry? Expected: Any nearby receiver can passively sniff packets without leaving a digital trace. Why can't a basic Micro:bit use military-grade 256-bit AES encryption? Expected: The Micro:bit's microcontroller has limited RAM and processing power; heavy cryptographic algorithms would cause memory exhaustion and battery depletion.

lessons.title: Revision: Structured Data & Data Validation
lessons.learningGoal: Explain how structured data formats and validation rules safeguard data integrity in Micro:bit digital systems.

orientate.smartStart: In your workbook, identify the three essential pillars of data quality (Accuracy, Consistency, Completeness) and match each to a real-world error example.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain how structured data formats and validation rules safeguard data integrity in Micro:bit systems

activities.title: Technical Vocabulary: Data Quality & Structures
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the precise QCAA technical terminology required for Assessment 2. Model the distinction between data integrity (the overall condition of the dataset) and data validation (the automated check implemented to maintain integrity). Emphasise that for term-matching questions, students must distinguish state from process.
activities.studentsDo: Read each locked term in column 1. Select the matching definition from the scrambled bank at the bottom of the table and write the matching letter into the blank cell.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each data term in the table to its correct definition from the definition bank below. Write the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why is data integrity classified as a condition rather than a process? Expected: Because integrity describes the actual state of data being accurate, complete, and consistent, whereas validation is the operational process used to preserve it.
What happens to data completeness if a sensor cable disconnects intermittently during logging? Expected: Missing values or null records will be introduced, leaving gaps in the dataset and violating data completeness.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
A. Highly organised data arranged into fixed fields and records within tables or spreadsheets.
B. The overall state of data being accurate, complete, and consistent across its lifecycle.
C. Automated check enforcing constraints on inputs prior to storage or processing.
D. The degree to which data values match the true real-world measurement without error.
E. Uniformity of data formatting, structure, and naming conventions across an entire dataset.
F. The state where all mandatory fields and records contain values with zero omissions.
activities.eLearning: Display master vocabulary slide on projector; students keep workbook flat on desks.
activities.transition: Now that our definitions are solidified, we will examine how these concepts connect within an algorithmic data logging pipeline.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Data Pipelines & Validation Controls
activities.teacherDoes: Work through the data validation pipeline on the whiteboard. Explain the roles of range checks, format checks, and presence checks using a wearable sports tracker scenario from St Brendan's College training sessions. Model how raw inputs must be filtered before insertion into Excel.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's explanation and fill in the missing technical terms in the guided notes cloze passage using the word bank provided.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze passage in your workbook by writing the correct term from the word bank into each numbered blank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is an impossible temperature reading of 210°C caught by a range check rather than a type check?
Expected: Because 210 is still a valid numerical integer data type, so only a boundary rule specifying minimum and maximum values will reject it.
question: How does enforcing a dropdown list maintain consistency in a multi-user dataset?
Expected: It eliminates spelling mistakes, capitalization discrepancies, and synonyms, ensuring identical categories are recorded uniformly.
activities.scaffolding:
Core validation checks:
- Range check: Rejects numerical values outside lower and upper limits.
- Type check: Ensures inputs conform to integer, float, text, or Boolean.
- Presence check: Blocks empty fields to guarantee completeness.
- List/Lookup check: Restricts entry to predefined permitted values.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed; all eyes on board during teacher modelling.
activities.transition: Let us now apply these validation mechanisms to design an input specification for a wearable Micro:bit athlete monitoring device.

workbookSpec.title: Principles of Data Validation and Quality
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in the blanks using the terms in the word bank.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. validation, 2. range, 3. list, 4. presence, 5. completeness, 6. type, 7. integrity
workbookSpec.text: To guarantee high data quality, digital systems enforce {{1}} at the point of data entry. A {{2}} limit prevents extreme or impossible sensor values, such as an athlete recording a heart rate of 450 bpm. To ensure categorical uniform values across all records, a {{3}} constraint is used. When a system verifies that no mandatory field is omitted, it performs a {{4}} check, which preserves data {{5}}. In contrast, checking that a student ID contains only numerical digits is an example of a {{6}} check. Together, these rules safeguard overall data {{7}} across the system lifecycle.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. validation
2. range
3. list
4. presence
5. completeness
6. type
7. integrity

activities.teacherDoes: Present the wearable telemetry scenario: Year 8 St Brendan's students wearing Micro:bit devices during cross-country training. activities.questioning:
Why would an accelerometer impact reading of -50g be rejected if the sensor range is -8g to +8g? Expected: The physical sensor cannot physically measure -50g; such an entry represents transmission line noise and must be filtered out to preserve accuracy.
What validation rule best prevents unassigned records in a multi-runner tracking sheet? Expected: A presence check combined with a list check on Runner ID to ensure an authentic competitor is logged for every row.

2. Body Temperature (°C): 34.0–42.0
3. Session Active (Boolean/Text): TRUE/FALSE or ACTIVE/REST
Rule types: Range limit, List constraint, Format mask, Presence check.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Telemetry Validation Specification
workbookSpec.prompt: Determine the required data types, validation rules, and integrity purposes for the specified Micro:bit wearable sensor fields.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Step Cadence: Integer, Range Check (0-300), eliminates impossible human cadence values. Core Temp: Decimal, Range Check (34.0-42.0), prevents ambient sensor spikes. Runner House Group: Text, List Constraint (Bruton, Doyle, Hogan, Treacy), prevents misspellings.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Step Cadence: Data Type = Integer (Numerical); Rule = Range Check (0 to 300 steps/min); Purpose = Eliminates negative numbers and physically impossible human cadence values.
Core Temp: Data Type = Decimal/Float (Numerical); Rule = Range Check (34.0 to 42.0 °C); Purpose = Prevents ambient sensor spikes or faulty wire readings from distorting health analytics.
Runner House Group: Data Type = Text (Categorical); Rule = List Constraint ('Bruton', 'Doyle', 'Hogan', 'Treacy'); Purpose = Enforces consistency by preventing misspellings or non-existent house entries.

lessons.title: Revision: Binary Representation & Radio Protocols
lessons.learningGoal: Compare binary integer representation methods and evaluate broadcast versus direct wireless communication modes for Micro:bit devices.

orientate.smartStart: On your workbook mini-grid, calculate the 8-bit binary representation for decimal 45 using place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can convert decimal numbers to binary and contrast broadcast versus direct radio communication

activities.title: Vocabulary & Binary Conversion Grid
activities.teacherDoes: Model 8-bit binary conversion on the board using power-of-two headings (128 down to 1). Demonstrate converting the number 77: 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 01001101. Define bit, byte, and base-2 arithmetic. Review communication definitions: radio group, packet payload, broadcast, and direct addressing.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the binary conversion and networking definition table in the workbook by writing precise definitions and calculated bit strings.
activities.visibleInstructions: Define each technical term in the table below and compute the binary bit pattern for the listed sensor values.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do digital microcontrollers like the Micro:bit use binary instead of decimal internally?
Expected: Transistors and electronic switches operate reliably in two distinct physical states (on/off, high/low voltage), making base-2 the most physically robust representation.
prompt: What is the maximum integer value that an unsigned 8-bit byte can store?
Expected: 255 (calculated as 2^8 - 1, or 11111111 in binary).
activities.scaffolding:
Place value header: 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
Key definitions:
- Bit: The smallest binary unit of storage (0 or 1).
- Byte: An 8-bit sequence capable of representing integers 0–255.
- Broadcast: Unaddressed wireless transmission received by all devices on a radio group.
- Direct: Addressed wireless transmission intended for a single designated device.
activities.eLearning: Projector displays binary power-of-2 place value reference table.
activities.transition: With our binary foundation and networking terms established, let us explore how packets are transmitted wirelessly between Micro:bit units.

workbookSpec.title: Data Representation & Transmission Terminology
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the definitions and binary conversions required for Assessment 2 preparation.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Bit vs Byte: A bit is a single binary digit (0 or 1); a byte is a group of 8 bits capable of representing values 0-255.
Decimal 26 in 8-bit Binary: 00011010 (16 + 8 + 2)
Decimal 105 in 8-bit Binary: 01101001 (64 + 32 + 8 + 1)
Radio Group Number: A shared logical frequency channel (0-255) configured in Micro:bit code to allow devices to send and receive packets together.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Radio Packet Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Conduct a whiteboard comparison of radio transmission topologies. Explain that `radio.send_number()` in Micro:bit defaults to broadcast mode across the configured group. Compare this to direct addressed transmission where receiver logic inspects a target serial or device ID before processing. Highlight trade-offs regarding privacy, packet collision, and network overhead.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the lecture notes and fill in the missing technical concepts within the transmission cloze summary.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze summary on Micro:bit radio communication by selecting the appropriate terminology from the word bank.
activities.questioning:
What security risk occurs when medical or athletic data is broadcast over an unencrypted radio group? Expected: Any nearby receiver tuned to the same group can eavesdrop on and record the raw telemetry packets without authorization.
How does direct transmission reduce processing workload for devices not involved in a conversation? Expected: Receiver devices can quickly inspect the header address and discard packets not addressed to them, avoiding unnecessary algorithmic execution.
activities.scaffolding:
Key concepts:
- Broadcast = one-to-all communication; no recipient checking.
- Direct = one-to-one communication; uses device address or serial filtering.
- Overhead = metadata attached to packet (sender ID, sequence number, checksum).
- Interference = packet loss caused by concurrent transmissions on the same group.

workbookSpec.title: Micro:bit Radio Protocols and Topologies
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in each numbered blank using the provided word bank.

workbookSpec.text: Wireless data exchange on the Micro:bit uses 2.4 GHz {{1}} signals. When a device transmits without specifying a recipient, it uses {{2}} communication, meaning every device listening on that {{3}} receives the payload. This method offers high efficiency for emergency alerts but zero data {{4}}. In contrast, {{5}} communication targets an individual unit by checking a unique device {{6}}. While directed communication enhances privacy and avoids confusing other receivers, it requires additional packet {{7}} to manage addresses.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. radio
2. broadcast
3. group
4. privacy
5. direct
6. address
7. overhead

activities.title: Generative Analysis: Broadcast vs Direct Overlap Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Set up the overlap comparison: Year 8 Wearable Tech emergency muster beacon versus personal biometric heart monitor. Explicitly guide the criteria: transmission topology, security/confidentiality, code complexity, and battery/network overhead. Model how to categorise unique traits versus shared properties using the 2.4 GHz radio stack context.

activities.visibleInstructions: Record 3 exclusive features of Broadcast, 3 exclusive features of Direct communication, and 3 shared characteristics in the overlap organiser.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Which communication mode would you select for a whole-school fire evacuation alert beacon at St Brendan's, and why?
expected: Broadcast, because every wearable must receive the warning simultaneously without waiting for individual device handshakes.
prompt: Why might a high-density direct network suffer packet collisions during sports monitoring?
expected: Multiple Micro:bits trying to transmit simultaneously on the same frequency channel can corrupt packets, requiring retransmission algorithms.
activities.scaffolding:
Overlap prompts:
- Broadcast Only: One-to-many topology, anonymous receivers, zero addressing overhead.
- Direct Only: One-to-one topology, unique recipient filtering, protected individual data stream.
- Shared: Uses 2.4 GHz radio frequency, relies on radio group setting, subject to physical distance limits and interference.

workbookSpec.title: Broadcast vs Direct Communication Comparison
workbookSpec.prompt: Compare Broadcast and Direct wireless communication in Micro:bit systems.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Broadcast Only: 1. Transmits to all devices simultaneously. 2. No destination ID needed. 3. Zero privacy. Both: 1. Uses 2.4 GHz. 2. Range limited. 3. Requires matching radio group. Direct Only: 1. Targets specific ID. 2. Confidential data stream. 3. Higher packet overhead.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Broadcast Only:
1. Transmits to all devices listening on the active radio group simultaneously.
2. Requires no destination device ID or address header.
3. Offers no privacy; any nearby device on that channel can intercept the data.

Shared (Both):
1. Operates using 2.4 GHz Micro:bit radio signals.
2. Constrained by transmission range (10-20 metres indoors) and physical obstacles.
3. Requires devices to be configured to the same radio group channel.

Direct Only:
1. Targets a specific receiver using unique serial or device identification numbers.
2. Preserves data confidentiality for individual sensor feeds.
3. Adds packet overhead and filtering logic inside the on-received algorithm.

lessons.learningGoal: Apply deconstruction strategies and technical vocabulary to answer short-response and extended-response exam questions on data systems.

activities.title: I Do: Deconstructing Complex Exam Prompts
activities.teacherDoes: Project a 4-mark sample exam question: 'Explain how implementing data validation and direct radio transmission protects user privacy and data integrity in a wearable health monitor. Justify with two specific examples.' Explicitly model prompt deconstruction using the 4 callouts: 1) Identify cognitive verb ('Explain' - provide cause/effect mechanism; 'Justify' - give evidence); 2) Technical concept 1 (validation -> integrity); 3) Technical concept 2 (direct radio -> privacy); 4) Evidence requirement (two distinct examples). Model drafting bullet-point outlines before writing prose.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher think-aloud. Annotate the sample question in the workbook using callout numbers 1 through 4, recording the verb demands and required answer elements.
activities.visibleInstructions: Annotate the sample exam prompt in your workbook. Use the four numbered callout boxes to identify the cognitive verbs, technical concepts, and required evidence.
activities.questioning:
What is the penalty if a response defines validation accurately but omits the 'privacy' aspect of direct radio transmission? Expected: The student loses at least 50% of the available marks because the question requires explaining both mechanisms in relation to the scenario.
Why must an 'Explain' response contain connective words like 'because', 'therefore', or 'as a result'? Expected: Connective words establish the causal link between the technical feature and the resulting system benefit, fulfilling the cognitive demand.
activities.scaffolding:
Cognitive Verb Quick Reference:
- Identify: Name or state briefly.
- Describe: State characteristics or features.
- Explain: Give reasons, causes, and mechanisms (how/why).
- Justify: Defend a choice using evidence, trade-offs, and examples.
Response Formula: Claim -> Technical Mechanism -> Concrete Example -> System Outcome.
activities.eLearning: Projector displaying sample question callout overlay; students working in hardcopy workbooks.
activities.transition: Now that we have deconstructed the prompt structure, we will co-construct a high-scoring paragraph response together.

workbookSpec.title: Exam Prompt Deconstruction Stencil
workbookSpec.prompt: Practice Question: 'Explain how implementing data validation rules and direct radio communication protects data integrity and user privacy in a wearable fitness tracker. Justify your answer using two concrete examples.'
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Callout 1: Cognitive verbs 'Explain' and 'Justify'. Callout 2: Data validation rules ensuring data integrity. Callout 3: Direct radio communication preventing interception for privacy. Callout 4: Two specific wearable examples required.
workbookSpec.figureHint: Label callouts: [1] Cognitive Verbs, [2] Integrity Mechanism, [3] Privacy Mechanism, [4] Mandatory Examples Required.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Callout 1: Cognitive verbs 'Explain' (cause and effect / why) and 'Justify' (provide supporting evidence/examples).
Callout 2: Data integrity mechanism -> Data validation rules (e.g., range limits preventing corrupt values).
Callout 3: User privacy mechanism -> Direct radio communication (e.g., device addressing preventing eavesdropping).
Callout 4: Evidence requirement -> Two specific wearable examples (e.g., heart rate range check of 40-220 bpm; targeted packet transmission to coach's receiver ID).

activities.title: We Do: Co-Constructing Structured Exam Responses
activities.teacherDoes: Lead the class to co-construct an exemplar response to an exam question: 'Compare broadcast and direct radio communication, evaluating which is better suited for transmitting private heart-rate telemetry from an athlete to a coach.' Solicit sentence starters from students, refine terminology on the whiteboard (e.g., replace 'sends to everyone' with 'broadcasts unencrypted payloads across the common radio group'), and guide students to assemble a cohesive 6-line paragraph.
activities.studentsDo: Contribute technical points and vocabulary suggestions during class discussion. Record the co-constructed planning notes and final modelled response into the workbook sections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Collaborate with the class to deconstruct the comparison prompt. Record the agreed planning notes in Section 1 and transcribe the final co-constructed exemplar response into Section 2.
activities.questioning:
How does contrasting the addressing overhead of direct communication show higher-level evaluation? Expected: It demonstrates awareness that direct communication is not simply 'better'—it carries trade-offs in packet complexity and code implementation.
What specific phrase links our technical description back to athlete privacy? Expected: 'Direct transmission ensures biometric heart rate data is filtered by recipient ID, preventing unauthorized monitoring by other devices on the group.'
activities.scaffolding:
Paragraph scaffold:
1. Comparative Topic Sentence (state similarity and primary difference).
2. Technical analysis of Option A (Broadcast: group-wide, no filtering).
3. Technical analysis of Option B (Direct: addressed, confidential).
4. Justified evaluation in context (Why Direct is required for personal health data).
activities.eLearning: Classroom whiteboard used for live drafting; student laptops closed.
activities.transition: You have seen how an exemplar response is engineered. Now you will independently complete two exam-style questions under timed conditions.

workbookSpec.title: Co-Constructed Exam Response: Communication Comparison
workbookSpec.prompt: Compare broadcast and direct radio communication, evaluating which is better suited for transmitting private athlete heart-rate telemetry.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Deconstruction & Criteria Plan:
- Compare: Identify similarities (both use 2.4 GHz radio group) and differences (broadcast = unaddressed; direct = addressed).
- Evaluate: Judge suitability for private biometric telemetry with justification.

Co-Constructed Exemplar Response:
Both broadcast and direct communication transmit data wirelessly across Micro:bit radio frequencies. However, broadcast communication transmits packets to every listening device on the shared radio group without address filtering. In contrast, direct communication appends a unique device identifier to the payload, ensuring only the intended recipient processes the packet. For private athlete heart-rate telemetry, direct communication is substantially superior because it prevents unauthorized eavesdropping by other competitors on the course. While direct messaging introduces minor packet overhead, it protects personal health confidentiality and prevents data spoofing.

workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Question 1: Micro:bit microprocessors are built from digital electronic transistors operating in two distinct physical states (on/off, high/low voltage). Binary maps directly to these electrical states using 0s and 1s, ensuring reliable internal computation without signal degradation.
Question 2: A range check restricts input to specific boundaries (e.g., 0-250 steps/min), filtering out accelerometer glitches before storage to maintain dataset accuracy.

sections.label: Question 1: Explain why Micro:bit processors represent numerical sensor data using binary instead of decimal. (3 marks)
Question 2: Explain how a range check preserves data completeness and accuracy in a wearable step counter dataset. (3 marks)
Exam Readiness Audit: 3 topics mastered, 2 exam techniques to use, 1 final question.

activities.workbookMaterials: Workbook practice exam questions and audit sheet.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Question 1 (3 marks):
Micro:bit microprocessors are built from digital electronic transistors that operate reliably in two distinct physical states: on or off (high or low voltage). Binary (base-2) maps directly to these electrical states using 0s and 1s. This ensures reliable internal computation and memory storage without the signal degradation and electrical noise that would occur if circuits attempted to distinguish ten distinct voltage levels for decimal representation.

Question 2 (3 marks):
A range check sets strict minimum and maximum boundaries (e.g., 0 to 250 steps per minute) on sensor inputs. It preserves accuracy by intercepting impossible numbers caused by accelerometer glitches or loose wires before they are committed to storage. By pairing range validation with error flags rather than deleting rows, it ensures the dataset remains complete while preventing corrupt outliers from skewing averages.

Readiness Audit:
Student lists 3 mastered concepts (e.g., 8-bit binary conversion, range checks, broadcast vs direct radio), 2 exam strategies (e.g., underlining cognitive verbs, using cause-and-effect connectives), and 1 revision question.

lessons.title: Introduction to Computational Thinking & Sequence
lessons.learningGoal: Explain the four pillars of computational thinking and trace sequential algorithms in block code.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a match table in their workbook pairing everyday tasks (e.g. tying shoelaces, setting morning alarms) with precise step-by-step sequential instructions.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain the four pillars of computational thinking and trace step-by-step sequential algorithms

activities.title: Vocabulary of Computational Thinking
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly present the four pillars of computational thinking using concrete digital examples. Model the application: 'When building a digital wearable step-tracker, decomposition means breaking the project into sensor reading, screen display, and battery saving. Pattern recognition is noting that every step adds 1 to an accumulator. Abstraction is ignoring physical wrist strap colours to focus solely on sensor data. An algorithm is the exact sequence of code blocks executed line by line.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow explicit direct instruction, listen to the teacher's modelled examples, and complete the cloze sentences in the workbook using the provided word bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the blanks in the cloze sentences using the provided vocabulary bank in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is decomposition essential before writing any lines of code?
expected: It reduces complexity by breaking an overwhelming problem into small, manageable components.
question: How does abstraction differ from pattern recognition?
expected: Pattern recognition identifies recurring trends across data, whereas abstraction intentionally filters out unnecessary details to concentrate on essential logic.
activities.scaffolding:
Decomposition: Breaking down a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts.
Pattern Recognition: Identifying recurring trends or similarities within a problem.
Abstraction: Filtering out non-essential details to focus strictly on core logic.
Algorithm: A step-by-step set of precise instructions to solve a problem.
activities.eLearning: Project presentation slides to the board. Laptops closed and eyes on the board during explicit vocabulary instruction.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the four pillars of computational thinking, let us examine how instructions execute sequentially in Micro:bit programs.

To manage complexity, we utilise {{2}} to break a large project into smaller, granular components. When we observe recurring elements or trends in our design, we are applying {{3}}. Finally, we use {{4}} to concentrate exclusively on the essential logical components of a task while intentionally ignoring extraneous details.
