activities.title: We Do: Pair Programming and Device Pairing
activities.teacherDoes: Assign student pairs into Sender and Receiver roles with assigned unique radio groups (Groups 10–25 to prevent inter-team collisions). Direct students to open MakeCode, declare their shared key variable (e.g. key = 5), and implement the sender and receiver algorithms. Model the verification process on the projector: show how a sender inputs a value, adds the key, and transmits it, while the receiver catches the packet and reverses the operation. Monitor room to assist pairs experiencing radio channel mismatches or uncalibrated key variables.
activities.studentsDo: In assigned pairs, program one Micro:bit as the Encrypting Sender and the other as the Decrypting Receiver. Flash code to devices and execute the verification protocol, checking items off in the workbook as completed.
activities.visibleInstructions: Open laptops, connect Micro:bits, and program your devices. Verify your implementation by completing each step in the Radio Transmission Checklist.
activities.questioning:
prompt: If the sender transmits a temperature of 24 degrees with key = 5, what packet value travels through the air?
expected: The packet value 29 travels through the air as ciphertext.
prompt: How does a third Micro:bit on the same radio group without the key see this transmission?
expected: It receives the raw number 29 and cannot discern whether the actual temperature is 24, 19, or 29.
activities.scaffolding:
Pair Roles:
- Partner A (Sender): Button A pressed -> reads sensor -> adds key -> sends number.
- Partner B (Receiver): On radio received -> subtracts key -> shows number on LED matrix.
Debugging Rule: If display shows nothing, re-verify radio.setGroup().
Encryption Formula: Ciphertext = Plaintext + Key. Decryption Formula: Plaintext = Ciphertext - Key.
activities.eLearning: Students open MakeCode on laptops; teacher conducts active rear-of-room monitoring of coding environments.
activities.transition: Transition from practical device coding to evaluating communication reliability and cipher strength in workbooks.

workbookSpec.title: Radio Transmission & Decryption Verification
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify each technical milestone in your Micro:bit secure communication test.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 5 checklist items successfully verified through live physical testing between paired Micro:bit devices.
items: Unique radio group assigned and identical on both Sender and Receiver Micro:bits
Shared secret key variable defined and set to identical values on both devices
Sender successfully executes mathematical addition of key prior to radio.sendNumber
Receiver successfully intercepts packet and executes mathematical subtraction of key
Receiver LED matrix displays accurate, true sensor reading identical to Sender input

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 5 checklist items must be verified: 1. Matching radio group; 2. Matching key variable; 3. Sender addition logic; 4. Receiver subtraction logic; 5. Accurate LED output matching sender telemetry.

activities.title: You Do: Reliability and Cryptographic Limitations Evaluation
activities.teacherDoes:
Direct students to disconnect hardware and reflect on system constraints. Guide their focus toward distinguishing between network reliability (packet collision, physical distance) and data security (cipher susceptibility to brute-force). Model how packet loss affects decrypted values:
- Example for reliability: 'Reinforced concrete walls cause complete radio signal attenuation, resulting in dropped packets.'
- Example for security: 'Because the offset key is static, intercepting a single known temperature value instantly exposes the decryption key.'
activities.studentsDo: Independently complete the 3-2-1 written evaluation documenting factors causing radio failure and the cryptographic limits of their Micro:bit system.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 3-2-1 evaluation sections in your workbook: record 3 factors affecting wireless transmission reliability, 2 vulnerabilities of simple mathematical ciphers, and 1 real-world application where this level of security is acceptable.
activities.questioning:
q: What happens if a radio packet is partially corrupted by distance during transmission?
Expected: The receiver either fails to trigger the onReceived event (packet dropped) or receives a garbled integer, producing incorrect telemetry.
q: Why would this single-addition cipher fail in a commercial fitness wearable?
Expected: It is trivial to reverse; any eavesdropper observing numbers over time can spot baseline trends and deduce the secret offset key immediately.
activities.scaffolding:
Consider:
- Reliability factors: physical barriers, radio congestion/interference, battery voltage drop, distance/range.
- Security limitations: fixed offset key, vulnerable to deduction, no sender authentication.
- Safe applications: low-stakes school weather stations, plant soil monitors.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed; individual reflective writing in workbooks.
activities.transition: Call for pens down and invite two student pairs to demonstrate live decryption to conclude the lesson.

workbookSpec.title: System Reliability and Security Synthesis
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the transmission reliability and cryptographic limitations of your Micro:bit system.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Section 1 (Reliability): 1. Signal interference from competing radio groups sharing the same frequency band. 2. Physical attenuation and scattering from walls or human bodies. 3. Power drops from declining battery voltage reducing transmission output power.
Section 2 (Security): 1. Fixed key allows simple brute-force or algebraic deduction once plaintext-ciphertext pairs are observed. 2. Lack of sender authentication means any device can spoof valid transmissions.
Section 3 (Context): Low-risk environmental telemetry such as school weather stations or agricultural soil moisture monitoring where no private or financial data is compromised.

sections.label: 1. Three Factors Affecting Wireless Transmission Reliability
2. Two Cryptographic Limitations of a Fixed-Offset Cipher
3. One Context Where This System Provides Sufficient Security

activities.workbookMaterials: System Reliability and Security Synthesis Sheet
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Section 1 (Reliability): 1. Signal interference from competing radio groups. 2. Physical attenuation from walls/bodies. 3. Power drops from declining battery voltage.
Section 2 (Security): 1. Fixed key allows simple deduction once one reading is known. 2. No cryptographic authentication to verify the true identity of the transmitting sender.
Section 3 (Context): Low-risk environmental telemetry such as agricultural soil moisture alerts where financial or private identity data is not at risk.

lessons.title: Introduction to Wearable Technology and Sensor Audits
lessons.learningGoal: Classify wearable digital systems and justify sensor selections based on user needs.

orientate.smartStart: List three digital devices worn or carried on the human body, identifying one specific physical property each device detects.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can classify wearable devices and explain how their sensors capture data to meet user needs

activities.title: Wearable Systems Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly introduce wearable technology as a self-contained digital system worn directly on the body that samples environmental or physiological physical phenomena, processes that data, and delivers an interactive output. Write and model the foundational concepts on the board: Sensor, Telemetry, and User Interface. Emphasise that in digital systems, the sensor is the primary transducer converting analogue physical states into numerical signals.
activities.studentsDo: Read the term bank definitions and match each term to its definition in the workbook. Complete the third column by writing one concrete hardware component found in everyday wearables.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Match each term in column 1 to its exact definition in the bank by writing the corresponding letter (A, B, or C) into the Match column.
2. In the Hardware Example column, write the specific physical component used in a real wearable device.
activities.questioning:
Why can an electronic watch without sensors not be classified as an interactive wearable telemetry system? Expected: Without sensors, it cannot measure or capture physical data from the user or the environment to process and transmit.
How does telemetry differ from standard local data storage? Expected: Telemetry involves transmitting measured data wirelessly across a network or radio link to another system for logging and monitoring rather than merely keeping it local.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Sensor: Hardware transducer detecting physical properties (acceleration, optical pulse, thermal changes) and converting them to digital signals.
2. Telemetry: Automated wireless transmission of data measurements from remote source devices to receiving stations for analysis.
3. User Interface (UI): Hardware and software touchpoints (haptic motors, OLED displays, buzzer alarms) conveying output back to the wearer.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed and eyes on the front board while definitions and core system interactions are explicitly modelled.
activities.transition: Review answers as a class before transitioning to conducting a structured audit of commercial and athletic wearable systems.

workbookSpec.title: Core Wearable Systems Terminology
workbookSpec.prompt: Match each core concept to its system definition and provide an authentic hardware example.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Sensor: C (Hardware Example: 3-axis accelerometer)
Telemetry: A (Hardware Example: Bluetooth Low Energy antenna)
User Interface: B (Hardware Example: 5x5 LED matrix)
bank: A: Automated communication process where sensor data is measured and transmitted to a remote system.
B: The physical or visual hardware display and feedback mechanism connecting the human operator with the digital device.
C: An electronic input transducer that detects and measures physical quantities, converting them into digital numerical data.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Sensor: C (Hardware Example: 3-axis accelerometer, optical PPG heart rate sensor, or thermistor)
Telemetry: A (Hardware Example: Bluetooth Low Energy antenna, Micro:bit 2.4GHz radio module)
User Interface: B (Hardware Example: Micro:bit 5x5 LED matrix, piezoelectric buzzer, vibrating haptic motor)

activities.title: Wearable Device Input-Process-Output Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Model the Input-Process-Output (IPO) deconstruction of a commercial sports tracking vest used by the Yeppoon Seagulls Rugby League team. Think aloud: 'Input: 3-axis accelerometer measuring force in G-units and GPS tracking position coordinates. Process: Algorithm aggregates impact spikes exceeding 5G and calculates distance covered in metres. Output: Real-time telemetry sent to the coaching bench dashboard.' Guide students to complete the audit for two other devices.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the structured audit table in the workbook by deconstructing the sensor input, processing logic, and resulting output for each listed wearable device.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the blank cells for each wearable device: specify the exact sensor input type, the processing operation performed on that data, and the primary interface output.
activities.questioning:
What causes biometric sensor data such as heart rate or acceleration to produce errors when an athlete moves vigorously? Expected: Movement artefacts, sweat, or sensor displacement can distort optical readings and introduce sudden anomalous spikes.
Why must wearable devices filter or average raw sensor values before presenting them to the user? Expected: Raw sensor sampling produces high-frequency noise that must be smoothed to provide meaningful, legible metrics.
activities.scaffolding:
Available Sensor Inputs: 3-axis accelerometer (motion/impact), photoplethysmography (optical pulse), ambient temperature sensor, GPS receiver.
Processing Operations: Threshold checking (if value > limit), running average calculation, event counter (step tally).
Output Modes: LED indicator array, audible tone, haptic vibration, wireless data packet.
activities.eLearning: Display local context connection: Yeppoon Seagulls RLFC athletic performance tracking data requirements.
activities.transition: Direct students to turn to the comparative analysis activity to evaluate local community use cases.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Device Architecture Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Deconstruct the Input-Process-Output structure of commercial and applied wearable systems.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Seagulls Vest: Input = 3-axis accelerometer / GPS; Processing = Detect collision forces > 5G and calculate total sprint distance; Output = Wireless telemetry to sideline laptop / alert tone.
2. Sailor Tag: Input = Saltwater conductivity sensor / water immersion switch; Processing = Evaluates if circuit is closed by water for > 3 seconds; Output = 2.4GHz radio broadcast SOS beacon to boat receiver.
3. Heat-Stress Monitor: Input = Ambient temperature sensor / thermistor; Processing = Checks if temperature exceeds 36°C threshold; Output = Micro:bit 5x5 LED matrix displays warning icon and buzzer sounds.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Seagulls Vest: Input = 3-axis accelerometer / GPS; Processing = Detect collision forces > 5G and calculate total sprint distance; Output = Wireless telemetry to sideline laptop / alert tone.
2. Sailor Tag: Input = Saltwater conductivity sensor / water immersion switch; Processing = Evaluates if circuit is closed by water for > 3 seconds; Output = 2.4GHz radio broadcast SOS beacon to boat receiver.
3. Heat-Stress Monitor: Input = Ambient temperature sensor / thermistor; Processing = Checks if temperature exceeds 36°C threshold; Output = Micro:bit 5x5 LED matrix displays warning icon and buzzer sounds.

activities.title: Ethical and Functional Requirements Comparison
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that wearable technology introduces distinct ethical responsibilities compared to stationary digital tools because wearables track personal, biological, and spatial data directly from human bodies. Model the tension between user benefit and user privacy using continuous location tracking as an exemplar. Walk around room to monitor student reasoning.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the comparative overlap analysis in the workbook. Identify requirements unique to athletic performance wearables, requirements unique to health/medical wearables, and shared constraints common to all wearable systems.
activities.visibleInstructions: Analyse the requirements of Wearable Athletic Trackers versus Medical Wearables. In the workbook, write requirements exclusive to Athletics, exclusive to Medical, and shared constraints.
activities.questioning:
q: Why are ethical data concerns heightened when using wearables in a school or club environment?
Expected: Wearables log sensitive identifiable data (such as biometric strain or real-time location) about minors that could be exposed if unencrypted.
q: How does physical form factor constrain the computational capability of a wearable Micro:bit?
Expected: Battery weight, device size, and lack of active cooling limit the complexity of algorithms and the frequency of wireless radio transmissions.
activities.scaffolding:
Considerations:
- Athletic Trackers: High impact resistance, water resistance against sweat, real-time telemetry streaming, rapid movement calibration.
- Medical Wearables: High measurement precision, clinical calibration, automated emergency dispatch, fail-safe redundancy.
- Shared Constraints: Low power consumption, lightweight ergonomics, secure user data storage, intuitive non-distracting user interfaces.
activities.eLearning: Circulate room and ensure all students are writing concrete engineering and ethical constraints into their workbook.
activities.transition: Direct students to pause writing and prepare for the Smart Finish written reflection.

workbookSpec.title: Athletic vs Medical Wearable Requirements
workbookSpec.prompt: Compare the technical and ethical requirements of athletic performance wearables versus personal medical devices.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Athletic Trackers Only: Impact-resistant casing for high-impact sports; rapid sampling rate for kinetic movement bursts. Medical Wearables Only: Certified clinical accuracy for diagnosis; 24/7 continuous monitoring with emergency escalation pathways. Both: Lightweight biocompatible materials, secure data encryption for personal health information, and strict battery efficiency limits.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Athletic Trackers Only: Impact-resistant casing for tackling/running; rapid sampling rate for kinetic bursts. Medical Wearables Only: Certified accuracy for medical dosage/diagnosis; continuous 24/7 reliability with emergency service links. Both/Shared: Lightweight compact power source (battery life); ethical handling and encryption of sensitive personal physiological data; skin-safe biocompatible materials.

activities.title: Assessment Task Deconstruction
activities.teacherDoes: Distribute Assessment 3: Wearable Tech Investigation Task Sheet. activities.title: You Do: Wearable Control Logic Flowchart
activities.teacherDoes: Model the algorithmic translation from User Story to Flowchart. Draw standard flow symbols: Terminator (Start/End), Process rectangle (Read sensor), Decision diamond (Is sensor value > threshold?), and Action output (Sound buzzer / Flash LED). Emphasise that wearable logic must loop continuously to sample incoming data. Instruct students to independently design their wearable's control algorithm in the workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Independently construct the logic flowchart for their wearable device in the workbook template. Ensure the flowchart contains an explicit sensor input read, a conditional decision diamond with defined Yes and No branches, and an output feedback action.
activities.visibleInstructions: Draw the control flowchart for your wearable system. Label the sensor reading, insert your specific numerical threshold into the decision diamond, and define what occurs on both the Yes and No branches.
activities.questioning:
q: What occurs in your algorithm if the condition evaluates to 'No'?
Expected: It loops back to the start of the sequence to sample the sensor again without triggering the output.
q: Why must a delay or pause block be integrated into a wearable sensor sampling loop?
Expected: Without a brief pause (e.g., 200ms), the processor samples millions of redundant readings per minute and rapidly exhausts battery power.
activities.scaffolding:
Flowchart Architecture Rules:
1. Ovals/Pills = Start / End of program routine.
2. Rectangles = Processes (e.g., Read Accelerometer X, Store in variable 'impactForce').
3. Diamonds = Decisions with distinct Yes and No exit arrows (e.g., Is impactForce > 3G?).
4. Rectangles = Output Actions (e.g., Show Warning Icon on LEDs, Transmit Radio string 'FALL').
5. Arrow Loop = Return arrow looping back to continuous reading.
activities.eLearning: Students work independently in workbooks. Teacher moves across desks checking logical branch continuity.

activities.title: Deconstructing User Story Syntax
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how agile development frames problems from the perspective of an authentic stakeholder. Write on the board: 'Weak: I want a fitness tracker.' Contrast with: 'Strong: As a Yeppoon Seagulls athlete, I want to track physical collisions and high-impact accelerations, so that I can monitor concussion risk and know when to seek medical assessment.' Deconstruct the three essential clauses: 'As a [role]' defines the specific end user; 'I want [capability]' defines the functional requirement; 'So that [benefit]' articulates the measurable value proposition and hardware necessity. activities.title: Ethical Principles in Physical Computing
activities.teacherDoes: Directly teach the four core ethical principles governing wearable technology: Informed Consent, Data Minimisation, Privacy, and Anonymity. Explain that wearable devices sit directly on human bodies, capturing continuous behavioral and physical metrics. Highlight the difference between capturing aggregate telemetry and sensitive personal data. Walk through each definition using QCAA terminology and provide explicit workplace examples from sports science and health monitoring. Model how to select the correct definition from the provided bank and pair it with the corresponding term.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the four locked ethical terms in the workbook table. Select the correct corresponding definition from the bank and write it into the blank Match column for each term.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each ethical term in column 1 to its correct definition from the bank provided below the table. Write the matching definition text into the blank cell.
activities.questioning:
Why is data minimisation particularly vital when programming battery-powered wearable devices? Expected: Collecting only necessary data conserves processing power and battery life while reducing the severity of any potential data breach.
What makes biometric sensor data collected without user knowledge an ethical violation? Expected: It breaches informed consent, negates user autonomy, and infringes directly upon personal privacy rights.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Ethical Definitions:
- Informed Consent: Explicit permission given by a user who clearly understands what data is collected and how it will be used.
- Data Minimisation: The practice of limiting data collection strictly to what is directly required to perform the intended function.
- Privacy: The right of individuals to keep their personal information and biometric habits free from unauthorized scrutiny.
- Anonymity: Ensuring recorded datasets contain no identifying information that can trace telemetry back to a specific individual.
activities.eLearning: Display key vocabulary slides on the projector. Laptops closed during direct vocabulary instruction.
activities.transition: Now that we have established these four foundational principles, let us examine how they apply directly to physical computing data storage.

activities.title: Guided Notes on Sensor Data Privacy

activities.title: Sensor Capabilities and Technical Mapping
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate how to evaluate sensor capabilities against project data requirements. Explain the operational limits of the Micro:bit v2 onboard sensors: Accelerometer (measures gravitational force and acceleration across X, Y, Z axes from -2000mg to +2000mg), Light Sensor (uses 5x5 LED screen matrix in reverse bias to report light level 0-255), Temperature Sensor (onboard processor temperature in degrees Celsius), and Touch/Button Inputs (discrete Boolean states: 0 or 1). Model how to select sample rates: high-frequency sampling (e.g., 50ms) for impact detection versus low-frequency sampling (e.g., 5000ms) for ambient temperature monitoring to preserve battery and memory.

activities.questioning: Why is a sampling interval of 100 milliseconds appropriate for detecting a tackle in rugby, but unsuitable for monitoring classroom ambient temperature? Expected: Fast athletic impacts occur within fractions of a second, whereas ambient temperature shifts gradually over minutes; high-frequency logging would flood memory with redundant data. What data type is output by the Micro:bit buttons versus the accelerometer? Expected: Buttons output Boolean states (pressed/not pressed), while the accelerometer outputs numerical integer vectors.
activities.scaffolding:
Micro:bit Hardware Specifications:
- Accelerometer: 3-axis motion (X, Y, Z), units in milli-g (mg) or gesture states (shake, freefall, 3g, 6g, 8g).
- Light Sensor: Ambient brightness via 5x5 LED screen, integer range 0 (pitch dark) to 255 (bright sunlight).
- Temperature: Core processor temp, range -20°C to +80°C.
- Push Buttons (A, B, Logo touch): Discrete binary state (True/False).

activities.title: Flowchart Syntax and ISO Symbols
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the four core ISO 5807 flowchart symbols required for physical computing algorithms. Model on the whiteboard using an athletic step counter: Oval (Terminator: Start/Stop), Parallelogram (Input/Output: Read Accelerometer), Rectangle (Process: stepCount = stepCount + 1), and Diamond (Decision: Is stepCount >= 1000?). Emphasise that every decision diamond must have exactly two distinct, labelled exit lines ('Yes' and 'No' or 'True' and 'False').
activities.studentsDo: Complete the flowchart symbol-to-function matching table in your workbook. Use the provided definition bank to match each shape to its correct computational role.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each flowchart symbol in your workbook table to its correct functional definition using the provided bank.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must every decision diamond have exactly two distinct exit branches?
Expected: Because boolean conditions evaluate to either True or False, and the microcontroller needs an unambiguous execution path for both states.
q: What happens if a flowchart omits a Start or End terminator?
Expected: The boundary of the program is undefined, making it impossible to determine when the algorithm initialises or terminates.
activities.scaffolding:
Symbol Definitions:
1. Oval (Terminator): Represents the start or end point of an algorithm.
2. Parallelogram (Input/Output): Represents data read from a sensor or sent to a display/actuator.
3. Rectangle (Process): Represents an internal calculation, assignment, or memory update (e.g. counter = counter + 1).
4. Diamond (Decision): Represents a condition check branching into Yes/No paths.

activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'In 30 seconds we move from symbol definitions to mapping the complete logic flow of your wearable solution.'

activities.title: Guided Wearable Logic Mapping
activities.teacherDoes: Model the construction of a wearable sensor monitoring loop on the whiteboard using a St Brendan's sports training hydration or temperature alert scenario: Start -> Initialise sensor -> Read temperature -> Decision: Is temp > 32°C? -> Yes: Play warning tone & show warning icon; No: Display checkmark icon -> Wait 2000 ms -> Loop back to Read temperature. Explicitly highlight the distinction between an infinite sampling loop required for wearable devices and a terminating linear program.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the guided flow structure in your workbook by filling in the blank stages for your wearable device, identifying the input sensor, the threshold condition, and the output actions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the blank nodes in your workbook flow map to represent your wearable device's primary sensor-checking algorithm.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do physical wearable devices typically loop continuously rather than terminating at an 'End' block?
expected: Because a wearable monitor must continuously sample environmental or biological data over time rather than shutting down after one check.
prompt: How can an algorithm be designed to prevent excessive battery drain during continuous loops?
expected: By incorporating a timed pause or standby state between sensor readings.
activities.scaffolding:
Standard Loop Structure:
1. Start (Oval)
2. Initialise variable (Rectangle: e.g. alertCount = 0)
3. Read Sensor (Parallelogram: e.g. read light / temp / acceleration)
4. Decision (Diamond: e.g. sensorValue > threshold)
5. Branching Action (Rectangle/Parallelogram: e.g. display alert)
6. Delay and Loop line back to Read Sensor.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate a manual logic trace on the whiteboard using a dry-run technique: place a marker on the 'Start' terminal and step through every possible input value (e.g. low sensor value vs extreme sensor value) to check for dead ends, hanging branches, or missing conditions. Model how to verify ISO 5807 compliance by asking: 'Does this decision diamond have exactly two distinct, labelled exit paths?' Direct students to conduct a structured audit on their own flowchart.

activities.questioning:
prompt: What is a 'hanging node' in a flowchart, and what happens when that is translated into MicroPython code?
expected: A hanging node is an unclosed path that does not lead to a subsequent step or loop-back, which in code results in a stalled or unhandled program state.
prompt: Why must sensor variables have explicit threshold units in decision diamonds?
expected: To prevent comparison errors between raw analog readings and scaled digital units, ensuring reliable conditional execution on the wearable hardware.
activities.scaffolding:
Verification Criteria Reference:
1. Exactly one Start terminal node.
2. All sensor inputs explicitly named (e.g. pin P0, accelerometer X, temperature).
3. Every diamond has two clearly labelled exit arrows (Yes/No).
4. All paths rejoin the main processing loop or terminate cleanly.
5. Output includes visual LED matrix or sound feedback for the user.

lessons.title: Translating Flowcharts into Structured Pseudocode
lessons.learningGoal: Write structured pseudocode using standardized keywords and indentation to represent conditional logic and sensor loops for a wearable digital solution.

activities.title: Explicit Pseudocode Conventions
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the formal syntax rules for algorithmic pseudocode. Model on the whiteboard: (1) Capitalise reserved keywords (SET, READ, IF, THEN, ELSE, ENDIF, WHILE, ENDWHILE, DISPLAY); (2) Use clear variable names (e.g. currentHeartRate, stepThreshold); (3) Apply 4-space indentation to define control blocks and nested statements; (4) Emphasise language-independence (do not use JavaScript braces or Python colons). Walk through converting a sample decision diamond into an IF-THEN-ELSE-ENDIF block.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze exercise in your workbook to define the core conventions of formal pseudocode syntax.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing terms in the cloze activity in your workbook to record the syntax rules of pseudocode.
activities.questioning:
q: Why are reserved keywords written in uppercase in formal pseudocode?
Expected: To clearly distinguish algorithmic control instructions from variable names and system data.
q: How does indentation convey scope inside an IF-THEN block?
Expected: It visually defines which instructions execute only when the preceding condition evaluates to True.
activities.scaffolding:
Pseudocode Rules:
- Reserved words: UPPERCASE (e.g. BEGIN, SET, IF, THEN, ELSE, ENDIF, LOOP, ENDLOOP).
- Variables: camelCase or snake_case (e.g. stepCount, light_val).
- Indentation: Indent all statements nested inside decisions or loops.
- Scope: Every IF must terminate with an ENDIF; every LOOP with an ENDLOOP.

workbookSpec.title: Pseudocode Syntax Rules
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in the blanks using the provided word bank to record the essential rules of pseudocode.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. uppercase
2. indentation
3. independent
workbookSpec.text: In formal pseudocode, all structural control instructions such as IF, THEN, and ELSE must be written in {{1}}. To show that instructions belong inside a condition or repetition loop, programmers use consistent {{2}}. Pseudocode is designed to be language-{{3}}, meaning it focuses entirely on algorithmic logic without using syntax specific to a single programming language like Python or JavaScript.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. uppercase
2. indentation
3. independent

activities.title: Co-constructing Algorithm Translation
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class in co-constructing a complete pseudocode algorithm from a flowchart on the board for a 'Wearable Heat Stress Monitor' (relevant to St Brendan's College athletes training in Yeppoon). Model the step-by-step translation process: 1. Initialisation (SET tempThreshold = 35), 2. Continuous Loop (WHILE running == TRUE), 3. Sensor Reading (READ tempSensor), 4. Selection Logic (IF tempSensor >= tempThreshold THEN DISPLAY iconWarning and PLAY alarmSound ELSE DISPLAY iconOk ENDIF), 5. Power-saving pause (PAUSE 2000 ms), 6. Termination (ENDWHILE). Emphasise strict indentation rules and capitalisation of QCAA pseudocode keywords.
activities.studentsDo: Collaboratively transcribe and complete the structured algorithm translation exercise in your workbook, ensuring all uppercase keywords and indentation levels match the class model.
activities.visibleInstructions: Translate the class Heat Stress Monitor flowchart into structured pseudocode in your workbook. Ensure keywords are capitalised and nested lines are indented.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do we initialise the variable 'tempThreshold' before the WHILE loop rather than inside it?
expected: Initialising inside the loop would redundantly re-declare the constant variable on every cycle, wasting processing cycles and risking memory allocation errors.
question: What structural error would occur if we omitted the ENDIF statement?
expected: The processor or reader cannot determine where the conditional action terminates and the main program sequence resumes, leading to syntax ambiguity.
activities.scaffolding:
Model Structure:
BEGIN HeatMonitor
  SET tempThreshold = 35
  WHILE TRUE
    READ currentTemp FROM temperatureSensor
    IF currentTemp >= tempThreshold THEN
      DISPLAY iconWarning
      PLAY soundAlarm
    ELSE
      DISPLAY iconCheckmark
    ENDIF
    PAUSE 2000
  ENDWHILE
END HeatMonitor

activities.visibleInstructions: Independently write the full pseudocode and the 3-2-1 exit reflection for your wearable tech project in your workbook. Ensure all control blocks are properly closed.
activities.questioning: How does your pseudocode handle sensor values that sit directly on your threshold limit? Expected: By using greater-than-or-equal-to (>=) rather than strictly greater-than (>), ensuring edge cases trigger the intended alert. Which specific sensor variable are you initialising at the start of your script? Expected: Specific declaration such as 'SET lightVal = 0' or 'SET stepTotal = 0'. Why is explicit indentation critical when nesting selection statements inside sensor loops? Expected: It visually defines the scope of each block, preventing logic errors and making nested conditions readable.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist for Independent Drafting:
1. BEGIN [ProjectName]
2. Variable initialisation (SET...)
3. Loop construct (WHILE TRUE or LOOP)
4. Input command (READ...)
5. Selection block (IF... THEN... ELSE... ENDIF)
6. Output command (DISPLAY... / SEND...)
7. Loop closure (ENDWHILE / ENDLOOP)
8. END [ProjectName]

workbookSpec.title: Independent Project Pseudocode Specification
workbookSpec.prompt: Construct the formal pseudocode for your wearable technology device based on your Lesson 1 flowchart, followed by the 3-2-1 exit reflection.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Example Wearable Pedometer Solution:
BEGIN Pedometer
  SET stepCount = 0
  SET targetGoal = 5000
  WHILE TRUE
    IF accelerometerGesture == SHAKE THEN
      SET stepCount = stepCount + 1
      DISPLAY stepCount
    ENDIF
    IF stepCount >= targetGoal THEN
      DISPLAY iconTargetAchieved
      PLAY celebrationSound
    ENDIF
    PAUSE 100
  ENDWHILE
END Pedometer

3-2-1 Exit Reflection:
3 Keywords used: BEGIN, WHILE, IF
2 Variables declared: stepCount, targetGoal
1 Question for coding: How do I handle debounce on the accelerometer shake gesture in MicroPython?

activities.title: Mapping Pseudocode to Block Categories
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate mapping pseudocode constructs directly to MakeCode block drawer categories on the projector: 'SET variable' -> Variables drawer; 'READ sensor' -> Input drawer; 'IF-THEN-ELSE' -> Logic drawer; 'DISPLAY' -> Basic / Led drawer; 'WHILE TRUE' -> Basic 'forever' block. Demonstrate how misplacing an initialization block inside 'forever' rather than 'on start' causes continuous variable reset bugs. Model the completion of the first row on the projector workbook interface.

activities.visibleInstructions: In your workbook table, match each programming category to its functional definition using the definition bank.
activities.questioning: Why must variable initialization occur inside 'on start' rather than 'forever'? Expected: 'on start' runs exactly once when powered, ensuring the variable establishes a baseline value without being repeatedly wiped out every millisecond. What is the difference between an Input block (oval/hex) and a Logic comparison block? Expected: Input blocks report raw real-time data from sensors, while Logic blocks evaluate conditions (like < or >) to produce a True/False result.
activities.scaffolding:
Category Mappings:
- Variables: Used for declaring and updating stored data (SET count = 0).
- Input: Used for reading sensors (accelerometer, light level, button press).
- Logic: Used for conditional checks (if-then-else) and boolean comparisons (<, >, ==).
- Basic: Used for execution loops (on start, forever) and screen outputs (show number/icon).

activities.title: Guided Prototype Construction and Debugging
activities.teacherDoes: Instruct students to open laptops and navigate to makecode.microbit.org. Guide students through assembling a base wearable sensor monitor. Model debugging a deliberate logic bug: demonstrate code where the light sensor threshold is reversed (e.g. 'if lightLevel > 50' instead of '< 50' for a night-time warning wearable). Walk through inspecting simulator readings, tracing variable states, and correcting the comparison operator.
activities.studentsDo: Open MakeCode. Follow the guided sequence to assemble the baseline sensor algorithm, then complete the debugging exercise in your workbook by identifying and correcting the missing syntax operators.
activities.visibleInstructions: Open MakeCode. Assemble the base sensor loop on screen, and fill in the missing code syntax in your workbook exercise.
activities.questioning: If the simulator LED screen remains permanently blank, which two logic areas must you inspect first? Expected: First verify that the sensor threshold condition is reachable in the simulator, and second confirm that screen output blocks are nested inside the True branch. Why is testing in the software simulator an essential step before downloading code to the physical Micro:bit? Expected: It allows rapid isolation of logic bugs without hardware or battery connection variables interfering.
activities.scaffolding:
Debugging Strategy (Find-Fix-Verify):
1. Find: Observe simulator behaviour—does it trigger under expected values?
2. Fix: Check relational operator (< vs >), variable initialization, and loop placement.
3. Verify: Test boundary values (e.g. exactly 50, 49, 51) to confirm expected output.

lessons.title: Iterative Design and Prototype Auditing
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate wearable technology prototypes against functional design criteria using an iterative testing framework.

orientate.smartStart: On the board, write down the three core technical subsystems of any wearable digital device (Input/Sensor, Processing/Logic, Output/Display). Check answers with your shoulder partner.

activities.title: Iterative Lifecycle Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the iterative design cycle (Plan, Create, Test, Refine). Emphasise that in Year 8 physical computing, iteration prevents catastrophic hardware failure. Provide the concrete example of a sports step-counter built on a Micro:bit: without a physical test phase, an engineer cannot tell if arm swings generate false positive step counts. Define iterative design, prototype, and evaluation.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze sentences in the workbook using the provided word bank to establish standard technical definitions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing words in your workbook cloze passage using the terms from the word bank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must the 'Test' stage occur under realistic wearing conditions rather than flat on a desk?
Expected: Real movement introduces mechanical vibration, loose connections, and unpredictable sensor noise that static desk testing cannot reveal.
question: What happens to project development if an engineer skips the 'Refine' phase after discovering errors?
Expected: The final product retains design flaws and fails to satisfy the user requirements.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Iterative Design: A cyclic process of prototyping, testing, analysing, and refining a product.
- Prototype: An early physical or digital model built to test concepts and technical feasibility.
- Evaluation: Assessing system performance systematically against pre-determined success criteria.
activities.eLearning: Project the iterative design cycle diagram on the main display while students follow along in their workbooks.
activities.transition: Now that we have defined the four stages of the cycle, we will deconstruct how to evaluate physical and algorithmic criteria.

Once a preliminary physical {{3}} is built, engineers must {{4}} the device under simulated user conditions. Finally, the team will {{5}} the hardware and code based on actual telemetry collected.

activities.title: Deconstructing Wearable Success Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to match real-world failure symptoms to specific QCAA assessment criteria: Ergonomics/Comfort, Data Integrity, and Electrical Reliability. Walk through an example: 'A user reports that the Micro:bit battery connector disconnects when bending the wrist. Which criterion failed?' (Electrical Reliability/Strain Relief). Guide students to complete the matching table.
activities.studentsDo: Match each wearable design criterion to its operational testing description using the definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: In your workbook, match each Wearable Criterion to its correct operational definition by writing the corresponding letter or definition text.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is battery pack placement considered an ergonomic issue as well as an electrical issue?
Expected: An unbalanced or heavy battery causes user discomfort and pulls on the wiring harness during arm movement.
prompt: How does data integrity differ from electrical reliability?
Expected: Electrical reliability ensures power stays on, whereas data integrity ensures the sensor values captured are accurate, clean, and meaningful.
activities.scaffolding:
Match Options:
A: The device remains securely fastened without pinching, skin irritation, or excessive weight imbalance.
B: Sensor telemetry remains free from floating values, mechanical noise, and false-positive spikes during movement.
C: Circuit connections, JST power plugs, and wiring remain intact and continuously powered under physical motion.

activities.title: Prototype Traffic Light Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how to write an actionable engineering refinement statement. Contrast poor feedback ('make it better') with precise feedback ('secure battery harness using 15mm Velcro strap to eliminate cable pull on JST header'). Direct students to audit their current project design against the three criteria using Green, Amber, or Red.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct an individual audit of your wearable design in the workbook table. Rate each criterion as Green, Amber, or Red, and write one actionable technical refinement strategy for each.
activities.visibleInstructions: Assign a status (Green, Amber, or Red) to each criterion for your wearable device. In the third column, write a specific, technical refinement step for any criterion that is not fully resolved.
activities.questioning:
If your prototype is rated Amber for Data Integrity due to erratic accelerometer spikes, what specific code or physical fix could resolve it? Expected: Implement a threshold buffer in MakeCode or dampen the Micro:bit mount with foam.
Why must every Amber or Red rating have a concrete refinement strategy before building? Expected: To prevent wasted construction time and avoid building known hardware flaws.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Ratings:
- Green: Completely verified, safe, and meets standard.
- Amber: Functional but with noticeable instability, risk, or user discomfort.
- Red: Critical failure; device will not operate or is unwearable.
Sentence Starter: 'To resolve [Criterion], I will modify the [hardware/code] by [action]...'

2. Sensor Data Integrity: Amber | Increase accelerometer threshold from >1024 to >1400 in MakeCode to filter out minor arm tremors.
3. Battery & Circuit Security: Red | Construct a dedicated battery sleeve using elastic tape to stop the AAA pack swinging and pulling the JST plug out.

lessons.title: Physical Prototype Assembly and Quality Assurance
lessons.learningGoal: Construct a physical wearable prototype by integrating Micro:bit hardware, power supply, and mounting materials safely.

orientate.smartStart: Identify two safety risks associated with wearable electronics (e.g. short-circuiting exposed pins on conductive fabric, cable strain on the JST battery connector). Record both in your workbook notes.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can safely mount my Micro:bit and battery pack into a wearable housing

activities.title: Hardware Mounting and Safety Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate under the document camera the correct assembly sequence for a wearable Micro:bit housing: 1. Position non-conductive backing (felt/foam/cardboard). 2. Secure the Micro:bit edge connector away from skin and conductive elements. 3. Route the battery cable providing 20mm of slack (strain relief) before anchoring the battery pack. Explicitly show the danger of placing sharp edge pins against foil or metal wrist straps.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, noting the key safety and mechanical mounting principles, and prepare their physical QA checklist workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the document camera demonstration. Track the application of strain relief to battery leads and the placement of non-conductive insulation.
activities.questioning:
Why must the battery cable have slack rather than being pulled taut across the housing? Expected: Arm flex and movement pull on tight cables, which tears the delicate copper wiring out of the JST terminal.
What would happen if the golden edge-connector pins touch a sweaty wrist or metallic bracelet? Expected: Moisture or metal causes a short circuit, resetting the Micro:bit or corrupting sensor readings.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Assembly Principles:
1. Non-conductive isolation: Insulate edge pins.
2. Strain relief: Maintain a loop of slack on battery wires.
3. Display clearance: Keep 5x5 LED matrix and A/B buttons completely uncovered.
activities.eLearning: Projector active with live document camera view of the assembly steps. Laptops shut.
activities.transition: We will now transition to verifying your physical components against our Quality Assurance Checklist before securing fasteners.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Quality Assurance Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify each physical assembly requirement before and during your prototype build.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 6 items verified, checked, and signed off prior to power-on.
items: Non-conductive barrier placed between Micro:bit edge connector and wearer
Micro:bit 5x5 LED matrix and A/B buttons remain unobstructed
Battery leads have at least 15mm of slack to provide strain relief
Battery pack firmly anchored so it does not swing or exert lever force
Wearable attachment (strap/clip) can be donned and removed independently
No exposed wiring or conductive metal touching active GPIO pins

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 6 checklist items must be ticked and verified by student inspection during build. Critical safety check: non-conductive barrier and strain relief must be strictly enforced before battery insertion.

activities.title: Guided Prototype Construction
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate actively from the rear and sides of the room as students begin assembling their physical housings using Velcro, felt, clips, and bands. Guide students step-by-step: Step 1: Secure the base strap. Step 2: Attach the Micro:bit mount. Step 3: Fasten the battery holder. Model corrective interventions publicly: 'Notice how Jack has secured his battery pack centrally on the forearm rather than on the wrist joint—this distributes mass much better.'
activities.studentsDo: Assemble the physical housing, mounting the Micro:bit and battery pack according to project specifications and ticking off the checklist items.
activities.visibleInstructions: Construct your wearable mount step-by-step. Follow the QA checklist. Check your partner's battery strain relief before securing the final adhesive or Velcro straps.
activities.questioning:
Where should the battery pack be located relative to the Micro:bit to keep the device comfortable and balanced? Expected: Closely aligned along the line of the limb or centrally mounted on the strap to prevent rotational drag.
How can you verify that the A and B buttons can still be pressed cleanly while wearing the device? Expected: Mechanically press both buttons with one hand while the unit is strapped on.
activities.scaffolding:
Construction Sequence:
1. Measure limb circumference and cut strap with 50mm overlap.
2. Fasten Micro:bit bracket.
3. Anchor battery cradle with cable relief loop.
4. Fit test on arm/leg.

activities.title: Standalone Power-On and Deployment Log
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through transitioning their assembled prototypes from USB tethering to independent battery power. Model how to securely insert the JST battery plug without stressing the solder joints on the Micro:bit edge connector. Emphasize verification of power stability during dynamic physical testing. For example, demonstrate checking that LED matrix brightness remains steady when the device is flexed or moved. Circulate the room to inspect for secure mounting, correct polarity in battery packs, and proper strap tension.
activities.studentsDo: Flash the compiled hex code to the Micro:bit via USB, disconnect the cable, and connect the battery pack. Fasten the wearable prototype securely to the intended body location. Perform movement tests to evaluate physical stability and continuous electrical performance, then document observations in the deployment log.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Verify your code is successfully flashed and unplug the USB cable.
2. Connect the battery pack securely via the JST plug.
3. Strap the prototype onto your designated testing limb.
4. Complete the 3-section evaluation log detailing physical fit, electrical reliability, and required adjustments.
activities.questioning:
Why might a Micro:bit display flicker or reset when switching from USB power to a battery pack? Expected: Voltage drop under load due to high resistance, partially depleted AAA batteries, or an intermittent JST connector contact.
What structural failure points are most likely when a wearable prototype undergoes rapid physical movement? Expected: Solder joint fatigue from flexing wires, strap attachment points tearing, or the Micro:bit sliding out of 3D-printed housings.
activities.scaffolding:
Troubleshooting Checklist:
- Blank Display: Check that the battery box switch is switched to 'ON' and AAA batteries are inserted with correct polarity.
- Reset Loops: Voltage sag indicates weak batteries; replace cells before final testing.
- Ergonomic Discomfort: Reposition straps to avoid pinching skin or restricting blood flow.
activities.eLearning: Students use MakeCode via USB to flash their final hex file onto the Micro:bit, verifying code integrity before untethered deployment.
activities.transition: Carefully pack away spare batteries, secure your physical prototypes in designated storage trays, and prepare workstations for pack-down.

workbookSpec.title: Prototype Standalone Deployment Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the real-world physical and operational performance of your assembled wearable prototype during untethered testing.

sections.label: 1. Physical Fit and Stability Under Motion
2. Standalone Electrical Performance (Battery & Display)
3. Immediate Hardware Adjustments Needed

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Physical Fit: Mount remained secure during steady walking, but showed slight rotational slippage around the wrist during rapid arm movements.
2. Standalone Electrical: Battery pack delivered consistent voltage; the LED matrix remained bright and the program executed without unexpected reboots.
3. Immediate Hardware Adjustments: Add a high-friction silicone backing strip beneath the main mounting plate to prevent lateral shifting during user movement.

culminate.smartFinish: Stand up wearing your prototype. On the teacher count, perform 5 jumping jacks or arm swings. Keep standing if your prototype remained attached and powered on.
culminate.summarise: Physical computing requires harmonising mechanical materials with sensitive electronic hardware. Good strain relief and non-conductive mounting protect your Micro:bit from physical and electrical damage.

activities.title: Analysing Sensor Noise and Hysteresis
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the MakeCode 'Show Console Simulator / Device' serial plotter on the projector. Move a Micro:bit wearing rig to show accelerometer telemetry. Show how normal human motion creates irregular spikes ('noise') that cross a single static threshold repeatedly. Model how adding a debounce delay (e.g., 'pause 250ms') or an upper/lower threshold band (hysteresis) prevents erratic false positives.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the live sensor telemetry stream. Identify where false-positive triggers occur on the live waveform and complete the diagnostic notes in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the live sensor waveform on the screen. In your diagnostic log, identify the difference between intentional signal and unintended sensor noise.
activities.questioning:
Why does a single 'if sensor > 500' check produce rapid double-triggers when a person takes one step? Expected: Human steps create an initial impact spike followed by harmonic bounce or vibration that also crosses 500.
How does adding a 200–300 millisecond pause after a trigger event solve this problem? Expected: It introduces a refractory period (debounce) where the code ignores impact echoes while the limb finishes its motion.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Algorithmic Concepts:
- Sensor Noise: Unwanted electrical fluctuations or minor ambient vibrations.
- False Positive: An erroneous event detection when the target action did not actually occur.
- Debounce / Cooldown: A deliberate algorithmic delay preventing multiple reads of a single mechanical event.
activities.eLearning: Projector displaying live MakeCode console with connected Micro:bit streaming real-time accelerometer and light telemetry.
activities.transition: We will now run controlled physical trials to log raw sensor values across three movement conditions.

workbookSpec.title: Sensor Diagnostic Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Analyse the causes of sensor noise and identify solutions.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Cause of False Positive: Sudden limb deceleration or physical vibration causes sensor readings to spike above the threshold value even when the user is not performing the intended target movement.
2. Role of Debounce Delay: It pauses execution for 200-300ms immediately after detection, allowing the physical vibration to subside before evaluating the sensor condition again.

activities.title: Controlled Movement Telemetry Testing
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through conducting 3 distinct physical trials with their wearable: 1. Rest / Stationary. 2. Moderate Target Motion (e.g. 10 normal paces). 3. High-Intensity / Unintended Motion (e.g. desk tapping, waving). Circulate and ensure students record both the actual physical events and the count detected by their current algorithm. Model an example audit on the board: if Trial 2 yields 14 counts for 10 paces, demonstrate how to document the +4 error discrepancy before adjusting code.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct the 3 trials in pairs (one tester, one recorder). Record actual physical actions versus code detections in the Telemetry Test Table. Calculate error differences collaboratively.
activities.visibleInstructions: Perform the three test trials wearing your device. Record the actual physical count versus the number registered on your Micro:bit display. Calculate the error difference.
activities.questioning:
question: During the stationary test, did your prototype register any counts? What does that indicate?
expected: If it counted during rest, the threshold is set too low or the sensor is picking up background noise/vibration.
question: If you took exactly 10 paces and the Micro:bit counted 18, what must you adjust in your logic?
expected: Increase the acceleration threshold value or introduce a pause delay after each step to prevent double-counting.
activities.scaffolding:
Testing Protocol:
- Trial 1: Stand perfectly still for 10 seconds (Target count = 0).
- Trial 2: Walk exactly 10 deliberate steps (Target count = 10).
- Trial 3: Shake hands vigorously for 5 seconds while seated (Target count = 0).

Calculation Guide:
- Error Difference = Algorithm Count - Actual Actions Performed.
- Pass: Exact match or zero false positives.
- Fail: Deviation greater than zero.
activities.eLearning: Students use MakeCode web editor and serial output or on-screen 5x5 LED display counters to observe real-time sensor values.
activities.transition: Review your error count column. We will now reprogram your thresholds to eliminate discrepancies.

activities.title: Algorithmic Refinement and Iteration Log
activities.teacherDoes: Direct students to implement code adjustments in MakeCode: 1. Modify the numeric comparison threshold (e.g. increase strength value from >1024 to >1400). 2. Add or adjust a cooldown delay block ('pause 300 ms'). Monitor students as they re-flash their Micro:bits and re-test Trial 2 to verify that error rates decrease. Model an example on the board: showing how a threshold increase from 1024 to 1350 eliminates jitter.
activities.studentsDo: Update block code in MakeCode, flash to Micro:bit, re-test the movement, and document the before/after iteration in the refinement log table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Update your threshold and delay blocks in MakeCode. Re-flash your Micro:bit, run a second test of 10 paces, and log your refined outcome in the workbook table.
activities.questioning:
q: What happened to the count accuracy when you raised the threshold?
Expected: False triggers from arm swings stopped, and only genuine forceful steps registered.
q: What is the danger of setting the threshold too high?
Expected: Gentle or slow steps are missed completely (false negatives).
activities.scaffolding:
MakeCode Modification Patterns:
1. Increase threshold: Change `acceleration (mg) > 1024` to `> 1350`.
2. Add refractory pause: Insert `pause (ms) 250` immediately after incrementing the variable.
3. Common error checks: Ensure your variable resets correctly between test cycles.
activities.eLearning: Rear-of-room monitoring to verify students are editing MakeCode logic blocks and downloading updated hex files.
activities.transition: Save your refined program as 'Wearable_Prototype_v2'. Complete your exit reflection.

lessons.learningGoal: Apply data collection protocols and sensor calibration techniques to ensure accuracy and completeness in wearable telemetry datasets.

activities.title: Core Pillars of Data Integrity
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the three core pillars of data integrity (Accuracy, Consistency, Completeness) in the context of QCAA Digital Solutions data collection protocols. Display a simulated raw Micro:bit acceleration dataset exhibiting anomalies: mixed units (g vs m/s²), null values from disconnection, and uncalibrated zero-offsets. Model how each flaw invalidates subsequent analysis by demonstrating an incorrect mean calculation on uncalibrated offset data.
activities.studentsDo: Record formal operational definitions for each data integrity term into the structured workbook table and match common sensor error types to their corresponding definitions using the provided term bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 'Pillars of Data Integrity' definitions table in your workbook. Write the exact operational definition for each term and match the error types.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do uncalibrated sensor baselines compromise data accuracy in wearable telemetry?
Expected: Without establishing a zero baseline, every subsequent reading carries a constant systemic offset error, invalidating absolute measurements.
prompt: What is the difference between an inconsistency error and an incomplete record?
Expected: Inconsistency means data exists but uses differing formats or units, whereas incomplete records contain missing or null values due to dropped packets.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Accuracy is the degree to which sensor measurements reflect the true physical state. Consistency requires uniform units, scales, and sampling intervals across the entire dataset. Completeness requires that no scheduled measurement timestamps or data fields are null or missing. Bank of definitions for matching: 1. Constant systemic offset from uncalibrated baselines. 2. Differing formats or conflicting units across timestamps. 3. Missing or null values resulting from dropped wireless packets.
activities.eLearning: Display the exemplar faulty CSV dataset on the main classroom projector, highlighting missing null values and mismatched acceleration units.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'In two minutes we move from defining integrity principles to constructing our standard trial protocol steps for the Micro:bit sensors.'

workbookSpec.title: Pillars of Data Integrity
workbookSpec.prompt: Define the three core pillars of data integrity that govern experimental Micro:bit wearable data collection and match the corresponding sensor error types.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Data Accuracy: Constant systemic offset from uncalibrated baselines. Data Consistency: Differing formats or conflicting units across timestamps. Data Completeness: Missing or null values resulting from dropped wireless packets.
bank: Constant systemic offset from uncalibrated baselines.

activities.workbookMaterials: Table widget for 3 data integrity definitions and error matching.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Data Accuracy: The extent to which collected sensor values correctly reflect the true physical phenomenon (Matched definition: Constant systemic offset from uncalibrated baselines).
Data Consistency: Ensuring all recorded entries adhere to identical measurement units, timestamps, and formatting rules (Matched definition: Differing formats or conflicting units across timestamps).
Data Completeness: The condition where every required sampling period contains valid data with zero null or dropped values (Matched definition: Missing or null values resulting from dropped wireless packets).

activities.title: Calibration & Sampling Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Walk through the four-stage testing protocol: Calibrate, Sample Rate, Validate, and Capture. Connect a demonstration Micro:bit to the projector, show the live accelerometer readings resting on the desk, and demonstrate how pressing button A zeroes the baseline reading before recording athletic movements. Model how to read the context of the sentence to select the correct technical term from the word bank.
activities.studentsDo: Fill in the missing technical terms in the guided cloze passage using the provided word bank to establish their baseline testing procedure.
activities.visibleInstructions: Read the testing protocol summary and fill in the missing terms using the word bank provided at the top of the page.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must calibration occur while the wearable device is in a known rest state?
Expected: It allows the software algorithm to calculate the gravitational resting offset (1g or 0g) so dynamic motion can be isolated.
q: What happens if the sampling rate is set too low for an athlete's sprint?
Expected: Rapid acceleration changes are missed between samples, creating aliasing and incomplete motion tracking.
activities.scaffolding: Word bank: calibrate, baseline, sample, validate, integrity. Rule: Step 1 zeroing = calibrate baseline; Step 2 timing = sample frequency; Step 3 check = validate readings. Full definitions: Calibrate means adjusting sensor outputs to a known standard; Baseline refers to the initial reference point; Sample frequency determines how often data points are recorded; Validate means confirming data accuracy; Integrity ensures data remains uncorrupted during collection.
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate the live serial graph in MakeCode to display real-time sensor fluctuation.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'Finalise your sentences in 60 seconds; next we turn these rules into a wearable pre-flight inspection checklist.'

activities.title: Pre-Trial Verification Checklist
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through setting up an actionable pre-trial audit. Show that in wearable tech, hardware mounting failure (e.g. loose strap) corrupts accelerometer data just as severely as coding bugs. Model checking battery voltage, securing harness mounts, and clearing legacy EEPROM logs by demonstrating a live system check on the projector: 'Notice how the serial monitor outputs zero-drift when the sensor is rigidly locked in place. If this reads outside tolerance, your telemetry is compromised before you even step onto the track.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a physical and digital pre-trial audit on their Wearable Tech device prototypes, ticking off each verification milestone in their workbooks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Inspect your Micro:bit wearable setup. Verify each mechanical and digital requirement on your checklist before signing off readiness for live trials.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is clearing previously logged flash memory essential before running a new project trial?
expected: Old sensor logs will mix with new trial data, corrupting the time series and causing false baseline readings.
question: Why does physical mounting tension affect accelerometer telemetry?
expected: A loose mount introduces mechanical vibration noise that does not reflect actual human body movement.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist components:
1. Mechanical: Secure strap, no sensor wiggle.
2. Electrical: Battery pack firmly seated with stable voltage.
3. Digital: Clean serial output, flash log cleared, sample interval set to 100ms.
activities.eLearning: Ensure students keep laptops open only for reading device serial status during hardware handshake.
activities.transition: Signal for clean-up: 'Return all devices to charging docks. Pack workbooks and prepare for the 3-2-1 exit check.'

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 6 items verified: 1. Physical mount rigid. 2. Battery stable. 3. Code compiled. 4. Memory erased. 5. Serial link active. 6. Calibration complete.

activities.title: Baseline Calibration & Benchmark Run
activities.teacherDoes: Guide student pairs through a synchronized 20-second calibration trial. Circulate around the room checking that students hold their wearable devices steady to establish the rest baseline. Inspect student screens to confirm the sensor readings hover within the expected resting window (approx. 0g to 1g depending on orientation). Model how to record exact values in the audit table.
activities.studentsDo: Work in pairs to run a 20-second baseline audit. Record observed resting values, check for anomalous noise spikes, and complete the baseline audit table in their workbooks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Mount your Micro:bit wearable device, run your 20-second rest calibration, and record your baseline sensor telemetry in the audit table.
activities.questioning:
If your accelerometer reads 2.5g while sitting motionless on the desk, what fault has occurred? Expected: The sensor orientation is inverted or calibration offset was not applied correctly in code.
Why should both team members inspect the real-time graph during the dry run? Expected: To confirm data is smoothly populating without connection drops before starting the physical activity.
activities.scaffolding:
Baseline checks:
- Resting acceleration: ~1000 mg (1g) Z-axis or ~0 mg X/Y axes.
- Temperature: ambient room range (22–26°C).
- Light level: steady reading between 0–255.

activities.title: Delimited CSV Import & Data Hygiene
activities.teacherDoes: Project Microsoft Excel. Model opening the CSV file, using 'Text to Columns' with a comma delimiter, and auditing the dataset headers. Show how extraneous metadata rows (e.g. serial timestamps or device serial numbers) corrupt charting engines if not removed. Demonstrate using Filter to check for text errors in numerical columns.

activities.questioning:
q: Why does raw CSV data often paste into a single column (A) when opened directly in some versions of Excel?
Expected: The software needs a delimiter rule (comma or tab) specified to split text into distinct data fields.
q: Why must metadata header comments be deleted before highlighting a range to insert a chart?
Expected: Non-numeric header rows prevent Excel from parsing the series values and produce broken axis labels.
activities.scaffolding:
Data hygiene rules:
1. Row 1 must contain short, clean column headers (e.g. Time_s, Accel_mg).
2. Rows 2+ must contain purely numerical values.
3. Delete empty trailing rows at the end of the file.

activities.title: Constructing Calibrated Time-Series Charts
activities.teacherDoes: Co-construct a clean time-series line graph in Excel with the class using a student's sample trial data. Explicitly demonstrate adjusting the vertical (Y) axis minimum and maximum bounds to eliminate dead space and reveal subtle motion trends. Model adding descriptive axis titles with units: 'Time (seconds)' and 'Acceleration (mg)'. Example: Setting bounds from 600 mg to 1600 mg rather than 0 to 5000 mg ensures the waveform occupies the full plotting area.

activities.questioning:
If your sensor values fluctuate between 800 and 1200 mg, why is an axis scale from 0 to 5000 mg problematic? Expected: It compresses the waveform into a flat line, obscuring meaningful peaks and troughs.
What role does the X-axis play in validating experimental trial duration? Expected: It displays continuous elapsed time, verifying whether the full 60 seconds was captured without data drops.
activities.scaffolding:
Chart formatting rules:
- Chart Title: St Brendan's College Wearable - Movement Type Telemetry over Time.
- X-axis: Elapsed Time (s).
- Y-axis: Sensor Metric + Unit (e.g., Vertical Acceleration (mg)).
- Bounds: Min = lowest reading - 10%; Max = highest reading + 10%.

activities.title: Technical Data Interpretation & Evaluation
activities.teacherDoes: Provide a structured analytical writing scaffold. Direct students to correlate visual graph features (peaks, troughs, plateaus, erratic noise) with the physical actions documented in their Lesson 2 Observation Log. Challenge them to explain whether anomalies represent real physical motion or sensor error. Model an exemplar response on the board: 'Primary Trend: The time-series graph illustrates a repeating rhythmic waveform between 10s and 45s, averaging 1450 mg...'
activities.studentsDo: Independently write a three-part technical interpretation in their workbooks: identifying the dominant movement trend, evaluating an observed anomaly with evidence, and reflecting on prototype reliability.
activities.visibleInstructions: Analyse your Excel graph. Complete the three analysis sections in your workbook, quoting specific numerical values and timestamps.
activities.questioning:
prompt: How can you distinguish between a deliberate athletic movement and sensor contact noise in your data plot?
expected: Athletic movement produces rhythmic, multi-point waves, whereas impact or contact noise appears as a single-point vertical spike.
prompt: Does your empirical data support your original user story requirements? Explain why or why not using your graph values.
expected: Students must cite specific threshold crossings (e.g. exceeding 1200 mg confirms step registration).
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence starters:
- Primary Trend: 'The time-series graph illustrates a repeating rhythmic waveform between [time] and [time], averaging [value] mg...'
- Anomaly Evaluation: 'An isolated anomaly occurs at timestamp [t] where acceleration spikes to [value] mg, which correlates with...'
- Prototype Reliability: 'The data indicates high/moderate reliability because baseline drift was limited to...'
activities.eLearning: Students view their finalized Excel graph on screen while writing their technical response.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'In two minutes we bring all findings together for our Checkpoint review.'

workbookSpec.title: Technical Telemetry Analysis & Findings
workbookSpec.prompt: Synthesise your experimental findings by linking your Excel graph features to physical trial observations.

Section 2: An acute anomaly occurs at 35.2s where readings spike to 2400 mg before dropping to 300 mg; this directly corresponds to the recorded foot stumble noted in the Lesson 2 physical log.
Section 3: Telemetry confirms the wearable prototype successfully detects ambulatory motion thresholds (>1200 mg) with sufficient clarity to support the step-counting user story, satisfying project criteria.
