lessons.title: Debugging and Refining Wearable Code
lessons.learningGoal: Debug logic and syntax errors in wearable Micro:bit algorithms using structured tracing and verification techniques.

orientate.smartStart: On the board, inspect three common program defects: an infinite while loop without an exit condition, a variable type mismatch assigning a string to a numeric threshold, and a missing sensor comparison operator. In your workbook, match each defect to its technical error category (syntax error, logic error, or run-time error).
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can debug logic and syntax errors in my wearable Micro:bit code using structured tracing

activities.title: Modelled Algorithmic Debugging
activities.teacherDoes: Project a buggy Micro:bit data collection script showing an accelerometer threshold failure and missing serial output call. Explicitly model the Find-Fix-Verify debugging routine. Step 1: Isolate the conditional block. Step 2: Trace variable states (acceleration magnitude vs threshold value 1024). Step 3: Insert the missing output statement to verify sensor telemetry streaming. Point out that without serial print verification, silent logic errors go undetected in physical computing prototypes.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the live code tracing demonstration on the main projector. In the workbook code snippet, identify the omitted telemetry command and fill the missing code hole {{1}} with the correct serial output command.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Trace the projected Micro:bit script alongside the teacher.
2. Identify the missing telemetry function on line 7.
3. Complete the hole {{1}} in your workbook code snippet with the correct output method.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it critical to stream live sensor readings over serial when debugging wearable algorithms?
Expected: Sensor inputs fluctuate dynamically in physical environments, so streaming serial telemetry allows us to see the exact numeric threshold causing a branch failure in real time.
question: What is connection between a compile syntax error and a silent logic error on a Micro:bit?
Expected: A syntax error prevents the script from compiling or downloading to the board, whereas a logic error compiles successfully but triggers the wrong output or actuator behavior.
activities.scaffolding: Find-Fix-Verify Protocol: 1. Find: Trace where variable states diverge from expected values. 2. Fix: Modify comparison operators or insert missing syntax. 3. Verify: Re-compile and check output. Common serial commands: serial.writeNumber(val), serial.writeLine().
activities.eLearning: Monitor from the rear of the classroom to ensure all students have their Micro:bit MakeCode or Python editors open without unrelated browser tabs.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that we are moving from teacher-led code tracing into collaborative peer error audits.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Sensor Telemetry Debugging
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in the missing telemetry function call on line 7 to stream live accelerometer readings over serial.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: serial.writeNumber

activities.workbookMaterials: Structured block/code debugging template with fill-in hole.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. serial.writeNumber or serial.writeLine. Model answer: serial.writeNumber.

activities.title: Collaborative Code Audit & Tracing
activities.teacherDoes: Pair students up and distribute the structured Collaborative Error Log. Model how to conduct a line-by-line trace of a partner's wearable code: check input trigger, boundary condition (>= vs >), variable initialization, and loop delay. Demonstrate completing row 1 on the projector using a sample wearable script where a step counter increment was placed outside an 'if' check. For example, explain: 'When tracing the sensor input, check if the variable is initialised before the loop; if not, the Micro:bit will throw an undefined behaviour or retain garbage memory.'
activities.studentsDo: Exchange wearable code scripts with an assigned peer. Trace the logic against your partner's project user story, identify two distinct logic or boundary errors, and record the line number, error description, and concrete programmatic correction in the table.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Swap code with your designated peer.
2. Trace their sensor loop line by line.
3. Record two identified faults and proposed programmatic fixes in your workbook table.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do boundary condition errors (such as using > instead of >=) often cause wearable sensor misfires?
expected: Exact threshold values (such as an exact target heart rate or step limit) will be ignored, causing delayed or missed alert states.
prompt: What role does a pause block play within a fast-looping Micro:bit wearable sensor routine?
expected: It prevents sensor jitter and stops the processor from flooding the buffer with duplicate sensor readings.
activities.scaffolding:
Collaborative Audit Criteria:
1. Trigger condition valid? Check if input parameters match design specs.
2. Threshold operator accurate? Verify >=, <=, >, or < usage.
3. Sensor sampling delay appropriate? Ensure >100ms pause is applied.
4. Variable reset mechanism present? Confirm accumulator states reset correctly.
activities.transition: Signal for students to return the audited code to its author and prepare for independent script correction.

workbookSpec.title: Peer Algorithmic Error Audit Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Record two isolated logic or syntax defects from your peer's wearable code along with precise corrections.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Row 1: Line 12 - Sensor threshold evaluated with incorrect strict inequality (> instead of >=) -> Change condition to reading >= 1024 to catch exact baseline triggers. Row 2: Line 24 - Buzzer display has no clearing command or delay -> Insert basic.pause(500) followed by basic.clearScreen() inside the condition branch.

activities.workbookMaterials: Collaborative Error Audit table in workbook.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Expected student responses must identify specific logic flaws: e.g., Row 1: 'Sensor threshold evaluated with incorrect strict inequality (> instead of >=)' -> 'Change condition to reading >= 1024 to catch exact baseline triggers.' Row 2: 'Buzzer/icon display has no clearing command or delay' -> 'Insert basic.pause(500) followed by basic.clearScreen() inside the condition branch.'

activities.title: Independent Algorithm Refinement
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate the room conducting one-on-one debugging check-ins. Verify that students implement the peer-identified corrections and re-flash their Micro:bit devices. Prompt students to articulate how their change directly improved the algorithmic efficiency or sensor fidelity of their wearable solution. Model a verbal check-in: 'When I look at your threshold logic, notice how a flat 50-degree cutoff creates jitter; let's trace how your debounce buffer prevents that rapid oscillation.'
activities.studentsDo: Apply the verified programmatic fixes to your wearable project code in MakeCode. Re-flash the hex file to your Micro:bit device, test with physical movement, and complete the Prototype Refinement Log in your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Apply your debugging fixes in your code editor.
2. Re-flash the program to your Micro:bit and test physical responsiveness.
3. Complete the two refinement log sections in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
How does simplifying nested conditional statements reduce latency on wearable microcontrollers?
Expected: Eliminating redundant branches reduces processor execution cycles per tick, allowing the Micro:bit to respond immediately to sudden sensor fluctuations.
Why must programmatic adjustments be documented immediately rather than at the end of the project?
Expected: It provides an auditable engineering trail proving iterative design and prevents forgetting the root cause of resolved defects.
activities.scaffolding: Section starters: 'Algorithmic Change Implemented: Modified the threshold logic from... to...'; 'Observed Functional Impact: When physically tested on the wrist, the device now...'
activities.transition: Power down Micro:bit battery packs safely and turn attention to the front board for the Smart Finish.

workbookSpec.title: Prototype Refinement Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Document the algorithmic modification applied to your wearable device and evaluate the observed functional result.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Algorithmic Change Implemented: Added a debouncing delay (pause 300ms) and updated the tilt boundary from >45 to >=30 degrees to capture moderate wrist tilts. Observed Functional Impact: Eliminated false duplicate step counts during sudden arm swings while maintaining 100% detection rate during standard walking movement.

culminate.nextSteps: Bring your physical prototype casing, straps, and mounting materials to Lesson 2 for physical design evaluation.

lessons.title: Evaluating Physical Design and Ergonomics
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate wearable technology prototypes against physical design criteria including ergonomics, durability, and usability.

orientate.smartStart: On your workbook quick-poll continuum, rate the wearability of a raw, unhoused Micro:bit taped to a wrist from 1 (Completely unwearable / unsafe) to 5 (Fully wearable / commercial grade). Write one structural justification for your rating.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can evaluate the physical design of my wearable prototype against ergonomic and durability criteria

activities.title: Physical Design Evaluation Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce and explicitly define the three foundational engineering criteria for wearable devices: Ergonomics (human physiological comfort, contouring, and weight distribution), Durability (structural resilience, impact resistance, and secure component housing), and Usability (intuitive accessibility of buttons, displays, and peripheral ports). Model how to match these terms against industrial design definitions using the table format.
activities.studentsDo: Study the provided definitions bank in the workbook. Match each design term (Ergonomics, Durability, Usability) to its exact definition in the table by writing the correct definition from the bank next to each locked term.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Read the definitions in the word bank.
2. Write the matching definition next to each locked term in your workbook table.
3. Verify all three pairs before checking with the class.
activities.questioning:
Why can a wearable device with flawless block code still fail completely in real-world testing?
Expected: If the physical housing causes skin chafing, slips off during motion, or restricts arm movement, the user will refuse to wear it regardless of how well the code runs.
How does durability directly influence the data integrity of wearable sensors?
Expected: Poor durability allows the Micro:bit or battery pack to jiggle or disconnect, introducing sensor motion artifacts, disconnected pins, and lost telemetry packets.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Ergonomics = Design focused on anatomical comfort, balance, and minimizing physical fatigue; Durability = Capability of structural materials to withstand mechanical stress, friction, and repeated motion; Usability = Ease with which the user interacts with buttons, reads LED displays, and operates the device.
activities.transition: With our criteria vocabulary defined, we now use a formal rubric checklist to audit our physical prototypes.

workbookSpec.prompt: Match each wearable design evaluation criterion to its correct technical definition from the bank.

2. Durability -> Capability of structural materials to withstand mechanical stress, friction, and repeated motion
3. Usability -> Ease with which the user interacts with buttons, reads LED displays, and operates the device

activities.title: Wearable Prototype Physical Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate a physical audit using an exemplar wearable prototype. Inspect the housing under four strict QCAA investigation checkpoints: anatomical contouring, mechanical fastener stability, button/LED clear line of sight, and cable strain relief. Emphasize that ticking a criterion requires observable physical proof on the desk.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a hands-on physical audit of your wearable prototype using the checklist. Check off each criterion successfully satisfied by your physical build and highlight any that fail the audit.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Place your physical wearable prototype on the desk.
2. Test each physical requirement (comfort, security, interface access, housing).
3. Tick the criteria met and circle any unmet requirements for iterative redesign.
activities.questioning:
q: What specific hazard occurs when battery leads lack mechanical strain relief inside a wearable case?
Expected: Repeated physical movement bends the delicate JST wires until internal metal fatigue causes sudden power loss or short-circuiting.
q: Why must the 5x5 LED matrix and Buttons A/B remain unobstructed in wearable prototypes?
Expected: The user relies on immediate visual feedback and physical actuation to control states without removing the device.
activities.scaffolding: Audit checkpoints: 1. Ergonomic fit (edges smoothed, no pinching). 2. Attachment security (strap retains position under 30 seconds of brisk movement). 3. Interface accessibility (Buttons A and B depress cleanly, LED matrix visible). 4. Enclosure robustness (battery pack and board immobilized).
activities.transition: Take your audit findings directly into your written evaluative reflection.

workbookSpec.title: Physical Wearable Prototype Audit Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Audit your physical wearable prototype against the investigation criteria. Tick items verified by physical testing.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 4 items verified through practical inspection; any unticked items form the basis of the immediate iterative redesign phase.
items: Ergonomic fit: Enclosure contours comfortably against the body without skin pinching or chafing
Fastener security: Straps or clips maintain fixed position during simulated active movement
Interface accessibility: Micro:bit Buttons A/B and 5x5 LED display remain unhindered and fully operable
Structural protection: Housing shields the microcontroller circuit board and provides battery wire strain relief

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 4 items should ideally be verified. For student prototypes in development, items not ticked become the explicit targets for the refinement plan in the next activity.

activities.title: Evaluative Critique & Refinement Plan
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to write an evaluative engineering critique using QCAA cognitive verbs (evaluate, justify). Project the sentence frames: 'The physical prototype successfully addresses [criterion] because [evidence], however it exhibits structural limitation in [area]. To resolve this, I will [actionable modification].' Guide students to structure their responses into Design Strengths, Structural Limitations, and Refinement Actions.
activities.studentsDo: Independently synthesize the audit results into a structured written critique. Formulate concrete physical modifications to improve durability, ergonomics, or usability before final project submission.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Review your checklist results from the previous activity.
2. Complete the three reflection sections in your workbook.
3. Detail specific physical adjustments (e.g., adding foam padding, reinforcing battery brackets, widening button cutouts).
activities.questioning:
q: How does justifying design tradeoffs strengthen the evaluation section of your digital technology folio?
Expected: It demonstrates critical thinking by explaining why certain compromises (e.g. adding weight to gain structural protection) were chosen based on user requirements.
q: What is the difference between a superficial complaint ('it broke') and a technical engineering critique?
Expected: A technical critique pinpoints the exact physical failure mechanism (e.g., shear stress at the strap eyelet) and proposes a material or structural solution.
activities.scaffolding: Section Starters: Strengths: 'The prototype effectively demonstrates ergonomic balance by...'; Limitations: 'Physical testing revealed a structural failure when...'; Refinement Actions: 'Prior to final submission, the housing will be modified by...'
activities.transition: Store physical prototypes in project tubs and open workbooks for the Culminate phase.

workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the effectiveness of your wearable physical design against project criteria, identifying specific limitations and planned engineering refinements.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Strengths: The 3D-printed curved baseplate conforms cleanly to the forearm with zero sharp edges, satisfying ergonomic criteria. Limitations: Rapid arm swinging caused the AAA battery pack to shift inside the chassis, creating intermittent power disconnects. Planned Physical Refinements: Incorporate a double-slotted velcro retaining strap and add 2mm EVA foam shims to immobilize the battery housing.

lessons.title: Finalising Wearable Project Documentation
lessons.learningGoal: Finalise and audit wearable technology project documentation against QCAA investigation criteria and technical reporting standards.

orientate.smartStart: Open your wearable technology project folder. Conduct a rapid 60-second evidence inventory. Check if your folder contains all four essential investigation artefacts: Scoped User Story, Annotated Block Algorithm / Flowchart, Sensor Telemetry Excel Graph, and Physical Testing Log.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can audit and refine my wearable tech documentation against QCAA assessment standards

activities.title: Investigation Folio Quality Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Project a high-achievement exemplar investigation folio alongside the assessment rubric. Explicitly deconstruct what distinguishes an exemplary submission from a developing one: clear user stories (As a / I want / so that), fully annotated code showing sensor input thresholds, clean Excel line charts with titled axes and units (e.g., Acceleration in mg, Time in seconds), and evidence-based evaluative reflections. Model how to audit folio files using the checklist.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's deconstruction of the exemplar folio. Audit your own project folio files against the four locked criteria on your workbook checklist, marking items as verified or flagging them for immediate revision.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Examine the projected exemplar folio standards.
2. Open your project files and check each component against the workbook checklist.
3. Tick completed items and highlight missing evidence or unfinished charts.
activities.questioning:
Why are annotated code screenshots mandatory in an engineering investigation rather than raw code exports alone?
Expected: Annotations explain the computational thinking, variable roles, and logic thresholds, proving that the author understands how the program operates.
How does labeling physical units (e.g. mg, °C, seconds) on telemetry charts protect data integrity in your report?
Expected: Without units, raw numerical data is ambiguous and cannot be validated against the original problem criteria.
activities.scaffolding: Folio Evidence Standards: 1. User Story: Agile format stating target user, functional need, and benefit. 2. Algorithm: Logic flowchart or annotated block code with explicit threshold comments. 3. Telemetry: Excel chart displaying empirical sensor data with title, axes, and units. 4. Evaluation: Detailed critique comparing outcomes against initial criteria.
activities.eLearning: Laptops open to project documentation folders; rear-of-room monitoring for on-task document review.
activities.transition: Now pair up for a structured peer review to verify evidence clarity before final adjustments.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Investigation Folio Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify the presence and quality of each required documentation component in your investigation folio.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 4 items must be verified with tangible folio artifacts. Any unchecked item represents an urgent gap to resolve during the independent editing block.
items: User Story & Scoping: Clearly defines persona, functional requirement, and expected benefit
Algorithmic Logic: Annotated block script or flowchart with explicit threshold callouts
Telemetry Analysis: Excel graph displaying real sensor data with complete axis labels and units
Iterative Evaluation: Documented debugging records, physical design critique, and refinement justification

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 4 items must be verified with tangible folio artifacts. Any unchecked item represents an urgent gap to resolve during the independent editing block.

activities.title: Structured Peer Folio Review
activities.teacherDoes: Pair students with a review partner. Guide them through the protocol of providing objective, constructive peer feedback. Model how to formulate targeted critique: instead of 'graph looks good', write 'Graph is missing the Y-axis label (Strength in milli-g); add this to make the telemetry interpretable.' Direct pairs to record actionable feedback in both sections of their workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Review your partner's documentation folder against the project user story and rubric standards. In your workbook, record specific, actionable advice for your partner, and record the constructive feedback you received from them.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Swap digital folios with your partner.
2. Check their user story alignment, code annotations, and graph labels.
3. Write actionable feedback for your partner and record the advice you receive.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is peer feedback on technical documentation more effective when linked directly to rubric criteria?
Expected: It provides objective, actionable correction steps rather than subjective personal opinions, directly improving report quality.
question: What should you check when verifying that code comments match the project user story?
Expected: Ensure the sensor thresholds, loop timing, and alerts directly deliver the user need stated in the user story.
activities.scaffolding: Peer Review Prompts: 'Does the graph include units?'; 'Are the conditional statements in the algorithm explained?'; 'Does the evaluation reference empirical testing data?'
activities.eLearning: Direct students to use cloud sharing or screen-sharing to view peer documents without file corruption.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is standardised file naming and formatting critical in digital technology project submissions?
Expected: It ensures document version control, prevents file loss across network systems, and meets professional technical publishing standards.
question: How does verifying data tables against graphs prevent inconsistencies in your final report?
Expected: It ensures that the numbers cited in written evaluations match the visual data displayed in charts, maintaining scientific credibility.

orientate.smartStart: Open your workbook to the Usability Match task and pair the four core usability concepts with their definitions.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can analyse usability principles, user experience factors, and ethical implications in wearable technology design

activities.title: Usability and UX Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the four core UX dimensions in wearable digital systems: Usability (ease of use and learnability), Ergonomics (physical interaction and comfort with the human body), Accessibility (inclusive design catering to diverse sensory or physical abilities), and Feedback (system communication informing the user of operational status). Modelled example: Contrast a smartwatch displaying a tiny 4pt font without vibration (poor accessibility and feedback) with a Micro:bit flashing an icon and playing a tone when a step threshold is reached at St Brendan's College sports training.
activities.studentsDo: Match each locked term to its correct definition in your workbook using the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write the matching letter (A, B, C, or D) next to each term using the definition bank in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is ergonomics especially critical for wearable devices compared to desktop systems?
Expected: Wearables physically contact the user's skin and body during motion, so poor ergonomics causes chafing, fatigue, or non-use.
question: How does real-time feedback enhance the user experience during athletic activity?
Expected: It immediately verifies that an input or threshold was registered without forcing the user to stop and examine complex data displays.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions provided in bank: A. Ease of learning and operating a system effectively; B. Designing hardware to fit physical human body movement and comfort; C. Ensuring digital systems can be operated by individuals with diverse capabilities; D. Sensory signals returned to the user confirming system actions.
activities.eLearning: Ensure student laptops remain closed while definitions and comparative examples are shown on the main projector.
activities.transition: Now that we have established our core usability vocabulary, let us apply these criteria to conduct a structured heuristic audit on a wearable prototype.

activities.title: Guided Usability Heuristic Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to conduct a formal heuristic audit on a sample Micro:bit wearable device (a wrist-worn posture and step monitor). Demonstrate evaluating four specific dimensions: Visual Display Clarity (5x5 LED matrix readability under sunlight), Physical Ergonomics (wrist strap tension and edge connector clearance), Auditory/Haptic Feedback (clarity of alert tones), and Button Accessibility (ease of triggering Buttons A and B while moving). Model recording a concrete observation for Visual Clarity: 'Pass - Scrolling text is legible indoors, but icons must be used for rapid outdoor comprehension.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the guided heuristic audit table in your workbook for the sample wearable, recording the status and a specific design observation for each dimension.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the audit table by recording the status (Pass or Needs Refinement) and writing a specific design observation for each usability dimension.
activities.questioning:
question: Why might a scrolling text alert on a 5x5 LED display fail outdoor usability testing?
expected: Scrolling text requires extended visual attention and is difficult to read while walking or running under bright sunlight.
question: How does unshielded hardware impact physical ergonomics?
expected: Exposed sharp pins and rigid battery edges chafe against the skin and loosen during movement.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit criteria guide:
1. Visual Clarity: Readability of 5x5 LED icons vs scrolling text under varying lighting conditions.
2. Physical Ergonomics: Mounting security, weight balance, and skin comfort.
3. Sensory Feedback: Distinct tones or vibrations confirming system events.
4. Button Accessibility: Ability to press inputs without slipping or releasing grip.
activities.eLearning: Project the physical wearable prototype under the document camera or display clear high-resolution photos on the board.
activities.transition: Having audited physical and interface usability, we will now examine the broader design impacts and ethical responsibilities of collecting human biometric telemetry.

workbookSpec.title: Wearable Prototype Usability Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Record the evaluation status (Pass or Needs Refinement) and an empirical design observation for each usability dimension of the sample wearable.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Visual Display Clarity: Needs Refinement - Scrolling text takes 6 seconds to read; replace with instant static icon.
Physical Ergonomics: Needs Refinement - Sharp edge-connector pins touch bare skin; requires fabric foam backing.
Sensory Feedback: Pass - Distinct high-pitch beep confirms when threshold is reached without requiring visual check.
Button Accessibility: Pass - Button A is accessible with thumb; Button B requires slight wrist twist but functions reliably.

activities.title: Evaluating Design Impact and Ethical Implications
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through an analysis of the ethical and societal impacts of wearable biometric trackers. Model evaluating two key ethical dilemmas: 1. Data Privacy and Unintended Broadcast (unencrypted Micro:bit radio signals leaking movement patterns to unauthorized listeners); 2. User Consent and Autonomy (logging user telemetry without clear visual status indicators). Model an exemplar written justification connecting privacy principles to concrete technical mitigations.
activities.studentsDo: Independently complete the written evaluation in your workbook, analysing two ethical privacy implications and proposing two design modifications to ensure user privacy and physical safety.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the two written sections in your workbook: explain two ethical data implications and propose two concrete design modifications.
activities.questioning: What ethical breach occurs if a wearable logs biometric data continuously without an active recording indicator? Expected: It violates informed consent and privacy because the wearer and bystanders cannot tell when data logging is occurring. How can an ethical engineer mitigate open radio packet eavesdropping in a public setting like a school gym? Expected: By implementing paired group IDs, channel isolation, or simple symmetric encryption on the payload before broadcast.
activities.scaffolding: Evaluation focus points: Data Privacy (open wireless transmission risks, data ownership); User Consent (visual recording indicators, start/stop control); Inclusivity/Safety (hypoallergenic materials, adjustable fastening for diverse users). Sentence starters: 'Continuous biometric monitoring poses an ethical concern because...' 'To protect user privacy, the digital solution must...'
activities.eLearning: Circulate room and monitor written responses, ensuring technical terminology (informed consent, data privacy, radio eavesdropping) is applied.
activities.transition: Ensure your written analysis is completed in your workbook as we move to our culminating synthesis.

workbookSpec.title: Design Impact and Ethical Evaluation
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the ethical implications and propose design solutions for continuous biometric tracking wearables.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Ethical Implication 1: Broadcasting unencrypted radio packets allows nearby devices on the same frequency to intercept personal activity telemetry without authorization. Ethical Implication 2: Continuous background sensor logging without a visible LED indicator infringes on user consent, as users cannot verify when telemetry is actively recorded.
2. Design Modification 1: Implement a dedicated status icon on the display to clearly signal when telemetry logging is active. Design Modification 2: Introduce a manual confirmation button press to authorize wireless data transmission rather than streaming sensor data automatically.

2. Propose two concrete design modifications (hardware or software) to address these ethical and user-safety concerns:

activities.workbookMaterials: Structured written evaluation sections for ethical analysis.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Ethical Implication 1: Broadcasting unencrypted radio packets allows nearby Micro:bits on the same channel to intercept personal activity telemetry without authorization.
Ethical Implication 2: Continuous background sensor logging without a visible LED indicator infringes on user consent, as users cannot verify when telemetry is actively recorded.
2. Design Modification 1: Implement a dedicated status icon (e.g., small flashing dot) on the 5x5 LED matrix to clearly signal when telemetry logging is active.
Design Modification 2: Introduce a manual confirmation button press to authorize wireless data transmission rather than streaming sensor data automatically.

lessons.title: Usability Testing and Peer Protocol Execution
lessons.learningGoal: Execute a structured usability testing protocol to evaluate user experience and gather actionable peer feedback.

orientate.smartStart: Power on your Micro:bit wearable prototype, attach your battery pack, and open your workbook to the Usability Protocol Checklist.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can execute a structured usability testing protocol to collect peer feedback on my wearable prototype

activities.title: Modelling the Usability Testing Protocol
activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate how to run a rigorous, objective peer usability test without introducing tester bias. Show the class how to deliver a standardised scenario brief ('Put on the strap and attempt to trigger an activity log entry') without revealing button combos or hidden gestures. Model recording exact user behaviours, completion latency, and verbal remarks on the checklist. Emphasize that the observer must remain silent while the user navigates the device.

Example script:
'Observer: Please complete the activity log entry sequence using the wearable prototype. I cannot answer questions or assist while you navigate.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow along in your workbook and review the four mandatory procedural steps of the testing protocol as demonstrated by the teacher.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the protocol checklist in your workbook. Tick each procedural step as the teacher models the testing routine.
activities.questioning: Why must the test administrator remain silent rather than guiding the user when they get confused? Expected: Giving verbal hints masks interface flaws that an authentic end-user would encounter in the field. What is the difference between objective usability data and subjective user impressions? Expected: Objective data measures observable actions (e.g., time taken, button press errors), whereas subjective data captures user opinions and reported comfort.
activities.scaffolding: Protocol Rules: 1. Explain the scenario, not the buttons; 2. Do not touch the device once handed over; 3. Record observable friction points (fumbling, hesitation, accidental presses); 4. Capture exact user quotes.
activities.eLearning: Project the testing protocol rubric on screen while demonstrating the test procedure with a student volunteer.
activities.transition: Now let us co-construct our feedback categorisation matrix so we can classify user friction accurately during testing.

workbookSpec.title: Peer Usability Protocol Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Tick off each mandatory protocol phase as it is modelled and applied during testing.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All four checklist items must be ticked in chronological order during the live peer test execution to ensure validity.
items: 1. Scenario Briefing: Explain user goal without explaining interface buttons or gestures
2. Task Observation: Watch the user attempt sensor triggering and readouts without assisting
3. Friction Logging: Record physical slips, visual hesitation, and system errors in real time
4. Debrief Interview: Collect user ratings on comfort, display clarity, and ease of use

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All four checklist items must be ticked in chronological order during the live peer test execution to maintain rigorous empirical testing standards.

activities.title: Co-Constructing the Feedback Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a guided practice activity where the class categorises common usability test observations into three core domains: Hardware/Ergonomics, Software/Logic, and User Interface/Display. Model an observation on the board: 'User shook arm vigorously 5 times but no count registered; Fix: Lower the accelerometer threshold from 2000mg to 1200mg.' Guide students to identify the correct category and draft precise, actionable engineering solutions for each modelled flaw.
activities.studentsDo: Collaborate with your partner to complete the feedback categorisation table in your workbook, sorting observed test issues into Hardware, Software, or Display domains and writing concrete design fixes.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the table by writing an observed user difficulty and a corresponding technical fix for each of the three locked categories.
activities.questioning: If a user fails to notice that their radio data packet was rejected, is this a Software or an Interface problem? Expected: It is an Interface/Feedback issue because the system failed to communicate its internal status to the user. How should a design fix be worded in formal technical documentation? Expected: As an actionable engineering statement with specific components and parameters, rather than a vague complaint.
activities.scaffolding: Categories: Hardware/Ergonomics (strap security, weight, sharp edges); Software/Logic (threshold sensitivity, loop timings, radio channels); User Interface/Display (LED readability, icon recognition, buzzer audio pitch).
activities.eLearning: Display the shared matrix template on the board while monitoring student table entries.
activities.transition: With our classification system defined, pair up with your designated testing partner and execute the live usability protocol.

workbookSpec.title: Usability Feedback Categorisation Matrix
workbookSpec.prompt: Classify observed user difficulties into the designated technical categories and record an actionable design fix for each.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Hardware / Ergonomics: Battery pack swings loose during arm movement -> Secure battery pack with secondary elastic band behind the wrist mount.
Software / Algorithmic Logic: False step counts recorded when user simply turns wrist -> Increase shake threshold filter and add 300ms debounce delay.
User Interface / Sensory Display: User confused whether radio send succeeded -> Flash checkmark icon on 5x5 LED matrix and sound high C tone for 100ms upon successful transmission.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Hardware / Ergonomics: Battery pack swings loose during arm movement -> Secure battery pack with secondary elastic band behind the wrist mount.
Software / Algorithmic Logic: False step counts recorded when user simply turns wrist -> Increase shake threshold filter and add 300ms debounce delay.
User Interface / Sensory Display: User confused whether radio send succeeded -> Flash checkmark icon on 5x5 LED matrix and sound high C tone for 100ms upon successful transmission.

activities.title: Independent Usability Testing Execution
activities.teacherDoes: Oversee the peer testing session. Circulate through testing stations ensuring students adhere strictly to protocol rules (no coaching, non-leading observation, objective notation). Intervene only if hardware safety is compromised. Direct students to document empirical evidence into their individual Peer Usability Test Findings record. Model targeted observation: 'Notice how I am recording the exact timestamp the user hesitated, rather than just writing that the menu was confusing.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct the usability trial on your partner's wearable prototype. Silently observe their interaction during the test tasks, record your observations, and write detailed qualitative and quantitative feedback in your workbook sections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Test your partner's wearable device. Follow the protocol steps, observe their actions without offering hints, and document your findings in your workbook sections.
activities.questioning: What specific behavioural cue indicated that the user experienced friction? Expected: Hesitation when looking for input buttons and repeatedly looking at the instructor for guidance. How will this peer observation inform your code or physical build in Lesson 3? Expected: It highlights the exact sensor threshold and strap mounting modifications needed before final submission.
activities.scaffolding: Sentence frames for test findings: 'The user experienced difficulty when attempting to...' 'The physical mounting shifted because...' 'To resolve this in the final prototype, the developer must...' Complete rubric criteria and observation parameters are displayed on the board.
activities.eLearning: Conduct rear-of-room monitoring while student pairs conduct testing and record handwritten notes in their workbooks.
activities.transition: Return tested hardware to its owner and ensure all written findings are recorded for tomorrow's final iteration build.

lessons.title: Final Wearable Solution Iteration and Assessment Preparation
lessons.learningGoal: Refine Micro:bit wearable hardware and software algorithms based on usability feedback to complete the final prototype.

orientate.smartStart: Review your Peer Usability Findings from Lesson 2 and write down the single highest priority bug or physical defect in your workbook.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can refine my wearable prototype code and physical build based on user feedback

activities.title: Modelling Technical and Physical Refinements
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to translate peer feedback into code and hardware refinements. In MakeCode, demonstrate modifying an algorithmic loop to add clear sensory feedback (e.g., adding basic.showIcon(IconNames.Yes) and a 200ms tone upon radio transmission). Physically demonstrate cable strain relief by looping the battery lead through the housing chassis to prevent disconnections during movement. Walk through the four items on the Final Refinement Verification Checklist.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's coding and physical assembly demonstration. Review the verification checklist items in your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration. Review the verification checklist in your workbook before modifying your project.
activities.questioning: Why is adding a transmission confirmation icon essential for user experience? Expected: Wireless radio packets are invisible; visual feedback confirms to the user that their data was successfully broadcast. How does securing the battery lead with strain relief protect the hardware? Expected: It prevents dynamic arm movements from snapping the fragile JST connector pins or pulling the cable loose.
activities.scaffolding: Checklist criteria: 1. Code Logic (calibrated threshold, responsive feedback loop); 2. Data Transmission (verified radio group and packet structure); 3. Physical Ergonomics (secure strap, cushioned backing); 4. Hardware Integrity (strain-relieved battery lead, secure sensors).
activities.eLearning: Project MakeCode editor showing the insertion of confirmation feedback blocks and threshold calibration logic.
activities.transition: Now that we have reviewed the required standards, let us prioritise our planned modifications to ensure critical functional fixes are completed first.

workbookSpec.title: Final Refinement Verification Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify each technical and ergonomic item before completing your final wearable submission.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All criteria verified and checked off to confirm production readiness.
items: Code: Visual or auditory confirmation feedback implemented for every user action
Code: Sensor threshold values calibrated to prevent false triggers during movement
Hardware: Battery lead and external wiring secured with strain relief
Ergonomics: Wearable housing padded and secured comfortably to the user's wrist or arm

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All four checklist items must be verified and checked off prior to final project submission, confirming alignment with investigation criteria and functional robustness.

activities.title: Prioritising Iteration Tasks
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through ordering refinement tasks using a ranking activity. Emphasize engineering triage: core operational functionality (sensor threshold and radio code) must take priority over ergonomic comfort, which in turn precedes cosmetic styling. Model an evaluation: 'If a wearable looks pristine with custom stickers but fails to transmit data to Excel, it fails the core functional assessment criteria.' Assist students in ranking four common modification tasks.
activities.studentsDo: Order the scrambled modification tasks in your workbook from highest priority (1 = Core Functional Fix) to lowest priority (4 = Cosmetic Detail) using the provided bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rank the four modification tasks from 1 (highest priority) to 4 (lowest priority) using the item bank in your workbook.
activities.questioning: Why must fixing a faulty sensor threshold or radio group take precedence over aesthetic casing decorations? Expected: The assessment criteria evaluate data collection, algorithmic logic, and transmission functionality; non-functional devices fail the primary investigation objectives regardless of appearance. Under what circumstance does an ergonomic flaw equal a functional failure? Expected: If the physical mount is so loose or uncomfortable that the user cannot wear it to collect valid telemetry.
activities.scaffolding: Priority hierarchy: Priority 1 = Core algorithm execution and radio transmission; Priority 2 = Hardware structural stability and sensor reliability; Priority 3 = User interface clarity and feedback; Priority 4 = Cosmetic styling and housing decoration.
activities.eLearning: Display the ranking prompt on the board and guide class discussion on task triage.
activities.transition: With your priorities established, proceed to independent implementation: update your code, flash your hex file, secure your hardware, and document your final build.

activities.title: Independent Prototype Finalisation and Verification
activities.teacherDoes:
Circulate during independent build time. Support students as they modify algorithms in MakeCode, compile and flash hex files via USB, and complete final physical assembly. Conduct spot audits on working devices against student priority rankings. Ensure each student completes their final solution verification record in their workbook.

Model an example verification entry on the board:
1. Final Software: Adjusted threshold to 1400mg and added debounce loops to stop false triggers.
2. Final Physical Build: Secured battery pack with industrial velcro and added a foam backing to prevent chafing.
3. User Needs Evaluation: The prototype now successfully tracks reps autonomously while remaining comfortable during high-intensity movement.
activities.studentsDo: Implement your priority fixes in MakeCode, download and flash the final hex file to your Micro:bit, complete physical housing assembly, and write your final verification entry in your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Flash your final program to your Micro:bit, finish physical construction, and complete the final verification record in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
What empirical test proved that your algorithmic refinement resolved the usability problem? Expected: Running a 30-second trial resulted in exactly 10 recorded steps without false triggers, and the receiver confirmed 10 received packets.

How did your physical modification improve ergonomics during actual movement? Expected: Adding the foam backing eliminated pin scratching and the velcro loop kept the device stable during arm swings.
activities.scaffolding: Verification steps: 1. Code compiled and flashed cleanly; 2. Micro:bit operates autonomously on battery power; 3. Sensor responds accurately to movement; 4. Visual/auditory feedback displays; 5. Physical strap remains stable during vigorous movement.

lessons.title: Structuring Technical Explanations & Justifications
lessons.learningGoal: Structure formal written explanations and justifications for digital tech solutions using the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework.

orientate.smartStart: Compare the two engineering justification statements displayed on the board and identify in your workbook which statement is valid, noting two specific reasons why.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can structure written technical explanations and justifications using the CER framework

activities.title: Technical Writing & Justification Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the components of the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) framework aligned with QCAA digital technologies criteria. Model how an engineering justification transforms an assertion into technical evidence: Claim (The wearable device reliably alerts users to excessive heat exposure); Evidence (In 15 test trials, the temperature sensor triggered the alert LED at 34°C within 1.2 seconds); Reasoning (The conditional selection statement evaluates the sensor register every 500ms, ensuring immediate user notification). Direct students to focus on the workbook definitions.
activities.studentsDo: Match each technical writing term to its correct definition in the workbook by writing the corresponding letter or text from the definition bank into the match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each technical writing term in column 1 to its curriculum definition from the bank by writing the matching definition in the blank column.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is an unbacked assertion insufficient in a technical evaluation?
expected: Without empirical test data or algorithmic proof, assertions cannot be verified against design criteria.
question: How does technical reasoning bridge empirical evidence and a claim?
expected: Reasoning explains the underlying algorithmic rules or physical hardware properties that cause the observed data.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Claim: A concise statement or conclusion that directly answers the design or evaluation question.
- Evidence: Objective data, metrics, or observations collected during testing (e.g. sensor values, event logs).
- Reasoning: A logical explanation demonstrating how computing principles connect the evidence to the claim.
activities.eLearning: Display the CER framework terminology slide on the primary projector.
activities.transition: Now that we have verified technical justification vocabulary, let's complete guided notes converting raw testing notes into structured CER sentences.

For example, explain that the claim establishes the primary assertion regarding system performance before numerical telemetry is introduced.

Expected: Claim.

Expected: Quantitative metrics prove that the physical hardware operated within the planned parameters.

activities.title: Constructing a Technical Justification
activities.teacherDoes: Present an authentic test scenario on the board: 'Micro:bit Step Counter Prototype Trial 4: Out of 20 low-intensity walking steps, 12 steps were recorded (8 dropped). In 20 running steps, 20 were recorded.' Model drafting the Claim, selecting the numerical Evidence, and formulating Reasoning that attributes the dropped walking steps to an acceleration threshold set above 1500 milli-g. Circulate the room to monitor student drafting.
activities.studentsDo: Write a three-part technical justification in the workbook sections (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) evaluating the wearable prototype's performance from the board scenario.
activities.visibleInstructions: Draft a formal CER justification in your workbook using the step-counter trial data shown on the board. Complete all three sections: Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning.
activities.questioning:
How do you translate 'the device failed when walking' into formal QCAA technical terminology? Expected: The prototype demonstrated low sensitivity during low-intensity movement due to an excessive conditional threshold.
Why must the reasoning refer back to the algorithm's conditional statements? Expected: To prove that hardware sensor inputs are directly governed by the programmed software logic.
activities.scaffolding:
Section starters:
- Claim: The Micro:bit step-counter prototype [successfully / partially] measures user steps because...
- Evidence: Testing logs demonstrate that during walking trials, the device recorded [x/20] steps, while during running trials it recorded [x/20] steps...
- Reasoning: This occurs because the selection condition requires an acceleration threshold of >1500 mg, which...
activities.eLearning: Display the raw test data table on the board. Ensure students are working independently in workbooks.
activities.transition: Put pens down and prepare your 3-2-1 reflection for our Smart Finish.

workbookSpec.title: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Justification
workbookSpec.prompt: Using the raw step-counter test log on the board, construct a formal technical justification for the wearable prototype.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Claim: The Micro:bit wearable prototype partially satisfies user requirements, accurately detecting running while failing to capture low-intensity walking.
Evidence: Test logs show the device recorded 20/20 running steps (100% accuracy) but only 12/20 walking steps (60% accuracy).
Reasoning: The conditional statement uses an accelerometer threshold of >1500 milli-g; walking generates peak forces below this threshold, preventing the iteration counter block from executing.

activities.title: Hardware Safety, Pack-Down, and Workspace Reset
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the proper physical computing decommission protocol: disconnect battery terminals first, coil USB cables without bending pins, inspect Micro:bit edge connectors for wear, and return to kit slots. Monitor student execution across the classroom, verifying that all components are accounted for and stored correctly.
activities.studentsDo: Safely disconnect hardware, store sensors and battery packs, and complete the pack-down audit checklist in the workbook to ensure workspace reset is complete.
activities.visibleInstructions: Decommission your hardware following the four safety steps and tick off each item on your pack-down checklist.
activities.questioning:
Why must battery packs be disconnected before storing physical computing components? Expected: To prevent parasitic battery drain, short circuits, or accidental board damage while stored.
Why do we inspect the edge connector pins during pack-down? Expected: To check for mechanical bending, corrosion, or physical damage before the next practical use.
activities.scaffolding:
Decommission sequence:
1. Disconnect battery JST plug.
2. Coil USB cable gently without sharp bends.
3. Inspect edge connector pins and board for wear.
4. Place components securely in assigned storage bay.
activities.eLearning: Inspect hardware bays before signing off student pack-down checklists.
activities.transition: Direct students: 'Hardware safely returned and verified. Return to seats for our final unit wrap-up.'

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 4 items checked and verified with physical kit properly placed in storage bay.
items: Battery pack disconnected from Micro:bit JST connector
USB cables coiled neatly without sharp bends
Micro:bit board and sensors inspected for physical damage
Component kit returned to designated storage bay

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 4 items checked and verified with physical kit properly placed in storage bay.

lessons.title: Final Evaluations and Peer Review Synthesis
lessons.learningGoal: Synthesise peer feedback and evaluate project outcomes against functional criteria and user requirements.

orientate.smartStart: Open your workbook to the peer evaluation notes from Lesson 2: highlight the two most common technical suggestions made by your reviewers.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can synthesise peer feedback and write a comprehensive final evaluation of my wearable project

activities.title: Feedback Categorisation and Review Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how to deconstruct and categorise raw peer feedback into three distinct engineering domains: Hardware/Ergonomics, Algorithm/Code Efficiency, and Data Quality. Demonstrate transforming a vague peer note ('The strap fell off') into an actionable technical finding ('The wrist attachment lacked mechanical reinforcement, reducing sensor skin contact'). Write the modelled conversion on the board to guide student auditing.
activities.studentsDo: Audit and sort the peer feedback received during presentations into the three technical domains on the checklist, verifying that all items meet the necessary criteria.
activities.visibleInstructions: Categorise your peer feedback notes into the three domains and tick each verification box in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
Why should we separate physical ergonomic feedback from software algorithmic feedback?
Expected: They address completely different subsystems—software modifications cannot fix poor physical mounting or bad sensor placement.
How does external peer critique eliminate developer bias?
Expected: The creator understands how the device is supposed to work, whereas external users test it without preconceptions, exposing real usability flaws.
activities.scaffolding: Domains for categorisation: 1. Hardware and ergonomic factors (mounts, casing, physical wear); 2. Algorithmic logic and threshold sensitivity (code execution, response times); 3. Data representation and telemetry output (readings, logging accuracy, storage).
activities.eLearning: Laptops down while teacher demonstrates categorisation model on the board.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'In 1 minute we will use our categorised peer feedback to write our 3-2-1 project evaluation.'

workbookSpec.title: Peer Feedback Categorisation Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify that your peer review notes have been categorised into the required engineering domains.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All three engineering domains successfully identified and verified with specific peer notes attached.
items: Hardware and physical ergonomics feedback identified and logged
Algorithmic logic and sensor response feedback identified and logged
Data collection, logging, and visualisation feedback identified and logged

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 3 items ticked, with corresponding raw feedback notes accurately translated into specific technical adjustments across hardware, algorithm, and data domains.

activities.title: Final Project Evaluation Synthesis (3-2-1)
activities.teacherDoes: Model the construction of a high-standard 3-2-1 evaluation on the board. Co-construct an entry with the class for '3 Strengths' and '2 Areas for Improvement' using precise technical terminology (e.g., conditional selection, accelerometer sampling rate, mechanical durability). Emphasise that reflections must reference user story criteria.
activities.studentsDo: Independently write their 3-2-1 evaluation in the workbook sections, integrating specific peer feedback and empirical testing observations.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 3-2-1 evaluation sections in your workbook: write 3 technical strengths, 2 peer-identified improvements, and 1 key digital systems takeaway.
activities.questioning:
question: What distinguishes an engineering strength from a basic operational feature?
expected: A strength explains how a technical feature effectively satisfied user requirements with high reliability.
question: Why must improvement proposals include technical reasoning?
expected: Proposed fixes must explain how specific algorithmic or structural modifications will solve the identified limitation.
activities.scaffolding: Prompts provided: Section 1 (3 Strengths: code logic, sensor integration, wearability); Section 2 (2 Improvements: based on peer critique); Section 3 (1 Takeaway: computational thinking insight).
activities.eLearning: Circulate room from rear; prompt students to replace general terms ('it worked well') with technical terms ('the threshold logic executed without lag').
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 'You have 2 minutes to complete your 3-2-1 synthesis before we conduct our final submission audit.'

workbookSpec.title: 3-2-1 Wearable Project Final Evaluation
workbookSpec.prompt: Synthesise your project outcomes and peer feedback using the structured 3-2-1 evaluation sections.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 3 Strengths: 1. Conditional logic successfully filtered out sensor noise. 2. Enclosure housing withstood drop tests. 3. Data logging executed at 50Hz without buffer overflow. 2 Improvements: 1. Add hardware debounce capacitor to input button. 2. Optimise display refresh rate to reduce power draw. 1 Takeaway: Physical computing requires iterative calibration between hardware tolerances and software logic.

sections.label: 3 Technical Strengths: Identify 3 components of your wearable solution that successfully met design criteria.
2 Areas for Improvement: Detail 2 specific modifications identified through peer review or testing.
1 Key Digital Systems Takeaway: Explain the most important engineering or data concept learned during this unit.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Responses must detail:
- 3 Strengths: Specific mentions of code logic (selection/loops), physical enclosure durability, and reliable sensor data capture.
- 2 Improvements: Concrete design or code fixes addressing peer critique (e.g., adding threshold debouncing, reinforcing strap mounts).
- 1 Takeaway: High-level insight regarding the interaction between physical computing hardware, algorithms, and real-world data collection.

activities.title: Final Submission Readiness and Artefact Audit
activities.teacherDoes:
Conduct an explicit walkthrough of the final assessment submission package. Detail the four required elements: 1. Scoped user story & problem statement; 2. Annotated block-code algorithms and flowcharts; 3. Excel sensor data graphs & analysis; 4. Synthesised peer and self-evaluation. Monitor independent student file organisation and submission checks.

Model an exemplar audit by displaying a complete portfolio on the projector. Point out specific evidence required for item 2: 'Notice how the block-code screenshot includes explicit comments explaining the conditional branching logic for the sensor trigger. Ensure your workbook matches this level of technical annotation before ticking off the second checklist item.'
activities.studentsDo: Audit their complete project workbook and digital portfolio against the submission checklist. Verify that all four components are fully documented, titled, and ready for teacher grading.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your workbook against the final checklist. Verify that each artefact is complete and tick the corresponding box.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is comprehensive technical documentation essential alongside a working prototype in engineering?
expected: Documentation provides verifiable evidence of the iterative design, algorithm logic, and testing cycles that produced the final outcome.
prompt: What occurs if sensor data visualisations lack labelled axes or units?
expected: The analysis loses credibility because data trends cannot be mathematically or contextually interpreted.
activities.scaffolding: Portfolio components checklist: Problem Definition & User Story; Algorithm Flowchart & Annotated Code; Sensor Telemetry Graphs (Excel); 3-2-1 Synthesis & Peer Feedback.
activities.eLearning: LMS portal open for file uploads; ensure all student files follow the required naming convention (e.g., Surname_WearableTech_Final).
activities.transition: Direct students: 'Complete your audit checks and ensure all files are uploaded before our final unit wrap-up.'
